readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Bangsamoro Commission for Senior Citizens to carry out senior citizen law and policy inside the region.

The Commission is to ensure the full implementation of laws, policies and programs on senior citizens, review them, and recommend action to the Bangsamoro Government. Its stated objectives run from recognizing the place of older people in society and supporting their full participation, to encouraging families and communities to care for them, to providing a comprehensive health care and rehabilitation system for disabled senior citizens, and to bringing the private sector in as a partner.

Beneath the objectives the bill provides for a site of office, an organizational structure, a Regional Director with stated powers, office personnel, and core programs. It is drawn to be consistent with the principles and objectives of the national Commission of Senior Citizens, and it defines a senior citizen by reference to Republic Act 9994 — any resident citizen at least 60 years old.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section builds from the Constitution — adequate social services, a rising standard of living, social justice, and the family’s duty to care for elderly members with the State assisting through programs and social security — and then to Section 23, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which requires the Bangsamoro Government to support the welfare of senior citizens and uphold the benefits and privileges they already enjoy.

The practical gap is enforcement. Senior citizen benefits are national law; whether an older person in a municipality in Basilan or Lanao del Sur actually receives them depends on someone regionally being responsible for seeing that they do, and no such office exists.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the region aged 60 and over.
Disabled senior citizens specifically, for whom a comprehensive health care and rehabilitation system is an objective.
Families and communities, whom the bill sets out to encourage in caring for older members.
Local government units, where community-based health and rehabilitation programs are to be established in every political unit.
The private sector, named as a partner to be actively sought.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for Senior Citizens, headed by a Regional Director
The Commission’s office personnel and core programs

funding.detail: No figure. The Bangsamoro Government is to appropriate a regular budget for the office and its activities, with the proviso that all national programs under the Act are funded by the national government. That proviso is the load-bearing part: most senior citizen benefits are national entitlements, so the bill funds the regional office and leaves the benefits themselves on the national ledger.

whatChanges: The region gains a commission responsible for senior citizen law and policy.
A Regional Director and office structure exist to review implementation and recommend action.
Community-based health and rehabilitation programs are to be established in every political unit.
The Commission is aligned with the national Commission of Senior Citizens rather than duplicating it.
readings.insight:
The proviso in the appropriations section does most of the work and repays reading twice. The Bangsamoro Government funds the office; the national government funds the national programs the office oversees. That is the right division on paper — the benefits are national entitlements — and it also means the Commission’s power is entirely one of oversight and recommendation. It can find that a municipality is not delivering the 20% discount or the social pension; it cannot fund either.

The drafting is untidy in a way a committee should tidy. The bill runs Section 4, then Section 5 headed "Objectives and Functions", and then doubles back to Sections 4.1 and 4.2 — which is where the Commission’s actual functions are set out. The functions of the body being created sit under a numbering that suggests they belong to the preceding section.

One small thing that dates the text: Section 4.2 has the Commission recommending actions and policies to the "Bangsamoro Transition Authority and Bangsamoro Government". The BTA was the interim body; the region held its first parliamentary election in 2025. A bill filed in November 2022 could not have known that, but the clause reads oddly now.

The measure was enhanced in March 2023 before First Reading, and referred to the Committees on Social Services and Development and on Finance in July 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates 2 parliamentary districts in the Special Geographic Area, where the region's enacted districting act gives it one.

The First District takes 34 barangays — the Pigcawayan group, the Midsayap group, Macasendeg, Dungguan, and the Pikit barangays of Bagoinged, Barungis, Bulol, Buliok, Gli-Gli, Kabasalan and Rajamuda. The Second District takes the remaining 29, covering the rest of the Pikit barangays, Tapodoc, the Carmen group and the Kabacan group.

Section 2 handles representation in 2 stages. Each district is represented by a member of Parliament; in the present term, 2 of the appointed members are assigned to the seats, and in succeeding terms each district is represented by a member elected or chosen through political party selection.
readings.whyProposed:
The Special Geographic Area holds about 192,000 people — more than several of the region's existing districts — and both the member's districting bill and the cabinet's give it a single seat.

The case for 2 is arithmetic. On the floor of 100,000 per district that both districting measures adopt, 192,000 people support 2 districts of about 96,000 each, which is marginal; on the regional average of roughly 148,000 per district, the area is substantially under-represented with one. This bill takes the view that 2 marginal districts are fairer than 1 oversized one.
whoIsAffected: The residents of the 63 barangays, who would have 2 representatives rather than one.
The region's other districts, whose relative weight falls if the Parliament's district total rises.
Political parties, which under Section 2 would choose the representatives in succeeding terms.
Members currently appointed to the Parliament, 2 of whom would be assigned to the new seats in the present term.
implementedBy: The Act is self-executing as to the boundaries; elections within them run under the Bangsamoro Electoral Code through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office and COMELEC

funding.detail: No appropriation. The measure draws lines and assigns seats.

whatChanges: The Special Geographic Area gets 2 parliamentary districts instead of one.
Its 63 barangays are divided into a First and Second District of 34 and 29 barangays.
Two currently appointed members would be assigned to the seats in the present term.
readings.insight:
This bill is the answer to a problem the enacted districting act creates and does not address. BAA 58 gives the Special Geographic Area a single Lone District for 215,433 people, against a regional average of roughly 148,000 per district — so a voter there carries about two-thirds the weight of a voter in Basilan or Sulu, making the area the most under-represented unit on the map. This measure, filed in December 2022, would have split it in two.

The arithmetic is tight and the bill does not show it. Both districting measures set a floor of 100,000 people per district; 2 districts here would run at roughly 96,000 each on the figures the Parliamentary Districts Act itself prints. That is below the floor, which is presumably why neither districting bill took the option — and it is also why the under-representation persists, because the floor was written for a region of large provinces and bites hardest on the one unit that is neither a province nor a city.

Section 2 is the provision a reader should slow down on, because it does something constitutionally awkward. It assigns the 2 new seats, in the present term, to 2 members "from those appointed" — reallocating sitting appointed members to districts they were not appointed to represent. And in succeeding terms it has each district represented by a member "elected or chosen through political party selection", which blurs the distinction the Electoral Code is built on: district seats are elected by the district, party seats are allocated by proportional representation. A district representative chosen by a party is neither.

The division itself follows the geography sensibly. The First District gathers the Pigcawayan and Midsayap barangays in the north with the Buliok and Rajamuda group; the Second takes the southern Pikit barangays with Carmen and Kabacan. That tracks the 2 natural clusters of the territory, and it is roughly the line along which the 8 municipalities created by BAA 41 to 48 also fall.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates the Pura Municipal Hospital in Datu Blah T. Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte.

It is the most modest of the hospital bills in its ask and the most expansive in its reasoning. The facility is to be built initially as an infirmary of at least 10 to 15 beds, operating under whatever capacity and capability the licensing standards personnel prescribe, with medical and office equipment and other required facilities provided. Upgrading to a higher facility with a larger capacity comes later, on the evaluation and recommendation of the Ministry of Health.

Section 5 does something the other hospital bills do not. The hospital serves primarily but not only the patients of Datu Blah T. Sinsuat: it may extend its services as augmentation and support to other existing medical facilities, for patients from adjacent municipalities and particularly the coastal areas of Maguindanao del Norte, when the need arises. A hospital charter that plans for its own catchment to overflow is unusual, and on this coast it is realistic.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note opens on the Qur'an — "And if anyone saved a life, it would be as if he saved the life of the whole people" — and then builds a documented case, with footnotes, from the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the 1987 Constitution, the Organic Law, a World Bank assessment of universal health coverage in the Bangsamoro, and reporting on the national shortage of public hospital beds. Its structural claim is maldistribution: over 60% of the country's hospitals are privately operated and concentrated in urban areas, which leaves municipalities like Datu Blah T. Sinsuat with little or nothing.

Then it names the event. On 28 October 2022, Severe Tropical Storm Paeng — Nalgae — hit Maguindanao del Norte, and Datu Blah T. Sinsuat took the worst of it. Landslide and flash flooding destroyed houses, livelihoods and lives; phone lines and electrical posts went down; the roads and bridges to neighbouring towns were destroyed or impassable. The municipality was cut off with trapped victims in its sitios and barangays, outside help unable to reach them, and no way to send the injured out. The note's sentence is that the local government and its health response units did everything they could "but could not effectively respond... because they had no local hospital."

The bill was filed weeks later.
whoIsAffected: The residents of Datu Blah T. Sinsuat, a coastal municipality that was cut off entirely during Severe Tropical Storm Paeng in October 2022.
Patients from adjacent municipalities along the coast of Maguindanao del Norte, whom the bill expressly allows the hospital to serve.
The municipal government and its health response units, which had no facility to treat casualties during the storm.
The Ministry of Health, which decides whether and when the infirmary grows into a hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — evaluation and recommendation for any upgrade beyond the initial infirmary, and the licensing standards the facility opens under

funding.detail: The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" but the filed copy names no amount. The enacted act did: BAA 67 appropriates ₱50 million from the Miscellaneous and Personnel Benefit Fund of the 2025 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, with later operations in the annual appropriations.

whatChanges: Datu Blah T. Sinsuat gains a hospital facility where it had none during the storm that cut it off.
The coastal municipalities of Maguindanao del Norte gain a facility expressly permitted to take their overflow.
Upgrading is delegated to the Ministry of Health's evaluation rather than reserved to Parliament.
readings.insight:
This is the one hospital bill Parliament enlarged. The filed copy asks for an infirmary of 10 to 15 beds; BAA 67 establishes at least 25 beds built to the Department of Health's minimum national standards. Set against the South Ubian and Sibutu bills, which asked for 50 beds each and received 25, a pattern emerges that is about a standard rather than about generosity: Parliament appears to have settled on 25 beds to national standards as the unit of a municipal hospital, and moved every bill toward it from whichever side it arrived.

Section 5 is the bill's own contribution and it survived intact. Writing an overflow catchment into a hospital charter acknowledges something hospital laws usually leave unsaid — that the map of who uses a facility is drawn by roads and boats, not by municipal boundaries. On a coast where a storm can sever a town in a night, it also means the hospital has a legal basis to treat people from the next municipality along without anyone having to decide whether it may.

The explanatory note is the most heavily evidenced in this batch, with 7 footnotes to the World Bank, medical journals and news reporting, and it is still the last 3 paragraphs that carry it. A measure argued from SDG targets and maldistribution statistics becomes unanswerable when it reaches 28 October 2022 and the sentence about a local government that could not respond because it had no hospital. The bill is dated weeks after the storm.

readings.whatItDoes:
This builds a register of skilled workers in the Bangsamoro, from the barangay upwards.

Every barangay in BARMM is responsible for registering the skilled workers in its area, onsite or online, and for setting its own plans and guidelines for gathering the information. The bill defines skilled workers as those with specialised skills, training and knowledge, and — for its own purposes — narrows that to work usually involving physical strength: it names carpenters, welders, plumbers, artisans, handweavers and drivers.

The register records name, ethnic affiliation, address, contact details, skills, trainings attended, certifications, employment experience, and any other necessary detail. No fee of any kind may be charged for registering.

The data then travels up a chain the bill sets out step by step: barangays submit to the municipal or city Public Employment Service Office, which consolidates and submits to the provincial PESO, which consolidates and submits to the Bureau of Employment, Promotions and Welfare of the regional labour ministry. Highly urbanised and independent cities consolidate separately. The Bureau is named the sole repository of data on all registered workers in BARMM.

The rest is data governance: a period of compliance, sharing of data for employment and data matching, a prohibition on unlawful processing, rules on access to the registry, and annual updating.
readings.whyProposed: The gap is that nobody knows what skills the region has. Employment services can only match people to work if there is a list, and the labour ministry’s market information system has no bottom rung. Building the register at barangay level is the bill’s answer: the barangay is the only unit that actually knows who in the community welds, drives or weaves.
whoIsAffected: Skilled workers across the region — the bill names carpenters, welders, plumbers, artisans, handweavers and drivers — who register free of charge.
Every barangay in BARMM, which carries the registration duty and must write its own guidelines for it.
Public Employment Service Offices at municipal, city and provincial level, which consolidate and pass the data up.
The Ministry of Labor and Employment’s Bureau of Employment, Promotions and Welfare, named sole repository.
Employers looking to hire locally, who gain a searchable pool.
implementedBy: Barangays, which register the workers
Municipal, city and provincial Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs), which consolidate
Bureau of Employment, Promotions, and Welfare, MOLE-BARMM, as sole repository

funding.detail: The filed bill has no appropriations section. It runs from annual updating straight to the separability clause and effectivity. Every barangay in the region is given a data collection duty, and the cost of discharging it is not addressed.

whatChanges: Every barangay must register the skilled workers in its area.
Registration is free — the bill prohibits charging any fee.
Data flows barangay → municipal or city PESO → provincial PESO → the regional labour bureau.
The Bureau of Employment, Promotions and Welfare becomes the sole repository for the region.
The registry is updated annually and access to it is regulated.
Unlawful processing of the collected data is prohibited.
readings.insight:
The data protection provisions are the most interesting thing here, and they are better than the bill is often given credit for: a prohibition on unlawful processing, rules on who may access the registry, and a defined purpose of employment matching. That matters because of one field in Section 4 — ethnic affiliation. Collecting ethnicity alongside name, address and contact details, in a region with this history, is a decision with consequences well beyond employment matching, and the bill collects it without saying why it is needed or restricting what it may be used for. A committee should ask.

The definition is the second thing. The bill defines skilled workers broadly and then, "for purposes of this act", narrows them to work usually involving physical strength. That leaves out the region’s teachers, nurses, technicians and IT workers — plausibly deliberate, since the target is the informal trades, but it means the registry will not be what its name suggests to anyone reading the title.

The third is the absence of money. Every barangay in BARMM is directed to design and run a data collection exercise, and no appropriation accompanies the duty. Barangays are the least resourced unit of government in the country, and an unfunded region-wide data mandate discharged 2,590 different ways will produce a register of uneven quality at best.

readings.whatItDoes:
This declares the Dimapatoy Watershed in Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, a protected area, and then sets out in detail what may not be done in it.

The prohibited acts run to 12 paragraphs. Illegal or unauthorised cutting or gathering of trees and plants of any species in the watershed and its environs. Gathering and burning dried plants and trees. Open burning of solid waste. Open dumping or burning of biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste. Transporting and dumping collected domestic, industrial or commercial waste in bulk anywhere other than a prescribed facility. Constructing or operating landfills, waste disposal facilities or groundwater reservoirs in the watershed or any part of it. Open dumping or burning in flood-prone areas within the watershed. Littering or dumping along its roads, canals, parks and establishments, or causing or permitting that. Discharging or depositing any waste pollutant into the watershed's water body, or anything that would impede its natural flow. Discharging or injecting anything into the surrounding soil that would pollute groundwater. Discharging regulated water pollutants without a valid discharge permit. And mining and quarrying activities.

Section 4 sets protective measures and Section 6 provides that omission of any watershed duty, and violations of Sections 4 and 5, carry fines and penalties.
readings.whyProposed:
A watershed is the catchment that supplies water downstream, and its protection is a question of what happens upstream rather than at the tap. Declaring one a protected area is the instrument for restraining activity in the catchment before the water is affected.

The list of prohibitions tells you what the actual pressures are: logging, waste dumping, landfill siting, pollutant discharge and quarrying. These are the ordinary uses a watershed near a populated municipality attracts, and the bill's answer is to name each of them.
whoIsAffected: Communities downstream of the Dimapatoy watershed who depend on its water.
Residents and businesses in the watershed area, subject to 12 categories of prohibited activity.
Waste haulers and local governments, which may not site landfills or disposal facilities in the catchment.
Mining and quarrying operators, excluded from the area entirely.
Holders of discharge permits, whose permits become the condition of lawful discharge.
implementedBy: The Bangsamoro Government through the protective measures in Section 4, with fines and penalties for violations of Sections 4 and 5

funding.detail: No appropriation. The Act works by prohibition and penalty rather than by spending, though the protective measures it requires would carry enforcement costs the bill does not quantify.

whatChanges: The Dimapatoy watershed becomes a declared protected area.
Twelve categories of activity become prohibited within it, including mining and quarrying.
Landfills and waste disposal facilities may not be built in the catchment.
Discharging regulated pollutants without a permit becomes an offence in the watershed.
readings.insight:
Banning groundwater reservoirs is the clause most readers would pass over and it is the one that shows the drafting was done by someone who understood the hydrology. A reservoir in a watershed is normally thought of as water infrastructure — a good thing — but constructing one in the catchment alters the natural flow the watershed exists to deliver and can concentrate contamination. Listing it alongside landfills as a prohibited construction is a judgement about the watershed as a system rather than as a reserve of trees.

So is the prohibition on gathering and burning dried plants. Clearing dead vegetation looks like tidying; in a catchment it removes the ground cover that slows runoff and holds soil, and burning it in place is how an upland fire starts. Most protected-area statutes prohibit cutting live trees and stop there.

The weakness is in Section 6. The Act says violations of Sections 4 and 5 "shall be meted with fines and penalties" without stating what they are. A prohibition without a quantified penalty is unenforceable until implementing rules supply one, and implementing rules cannot create penal liability that the statute has not defined. Compared with the registry's other environmental measure — the proposed Lake Lanao authorities, 1 of which can set administrative fines itself — this bill prohibits more precisely and punishes less definitely.

One piece of context the bill does not supply. Datu Odin Sinsuat is the municipality whose district hospital is the subject of Bill No. 146, which has 13 co-authors, and whose barangays were split into 2 new municipalities by BAA 54 and BAA 55. It is among the most legislated-about local governments in the registry, and this is the only measure that concerns its water.

readings.whatItDoes:
One amendment, in one section, to one line of a budget law. This rewrites Section 3 of BAA 22 — the Special Development Fund appropriations for 2020 and 2021 — to keep that money alive until 31 December 2023.

The extension is graded by what the money buys. Everything stays available for release and disbursement until the end of 2023. Infrastructure capital outlays may be obligated until then, with construction, inspection and payment allowed to run on to 30 June 2024. Maintenance and other operating expenses and other capital outlays may also be obligated until the end of 2023, with delivery, inspection and payment permitted until 31 March 2024.

The finance ministry issues the guidelines. That is the entire bill: 3 sections, 1 page, no appropriation of its own.
readings.whyProposed:
There is no explanatory note on the filed copy. The Special Development Fund is the money the national government committed to the region under the peace agreement, appropriated regionally for 2020 and 2021, and a cash-based budget makes an appropriation expire at the end of its year.

The unstated premise is that the money had not been spent. An extension bill is only ever filed because the alternative — letting the appropriation lapse and reverting the balance — would mean the projects it was meant to build do not get built.
whoIsAffected: Communities waiting on Special Development Fund projects from the 2020 and 2021 programs.
Ministries and offices holding unobligated or undisbursed balances from those years.
Contractors on infrastructure whose completion, inspection and payment window moves to mid-2024.
The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management, which writes the guidelines and administers the cash budgeting system.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management (MFBM) — guidelines for the cash budgeting system as amended

funding.detail: No new money. The bill extends the life of appropriations already made under BAA 22 rather than adding to them.

whatChanges: The 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund stays spendable through 2023 instead of lapsing.
Infrastructure work funded from it may be completed and paid up to 30 June 2024.
Operating and other capital items may be delivered and paid up to 31 March 2024.
readings.insight:
The interest in this bill is not in the text, which is 1 page, but in the sequence it belongs to. The same fund is extended again 11 months later by Bill No. 265, which pushes the 2020 to 2022 Special Development Fund to 31 December 2024 and then adds the phrase that matters more than any date: the money is to remain available "until fully expended or disbursed". A deadline replaced by a condition is a different instrument altogether.

Enacted as BAA 34 on 22 December 2022 — 9 days before the appropriations it rescues would have lapsed. Its companion, Bill No. 128, became BAA 33 on the same day. Budget extension bills in this registry are consistently passed in the last weeks of December, which tells you they are not planned instruments but responses to a year ending with money unspent.

What no document in this sequence contains is the amount. The bill moves a date; it does not say how much of the 2020 and 2021 Special Development Fund was still sitting there when the year ran out. That figure would answer the question the extension raises, and it is not in the law, the bill, or the index.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 127, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This rewrites Section 48 of BAA 23, the 2022 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, to keep the year's budget alive through 2023 — with personnel services carved out.

Everything except personnel services stays available for release and disbursement, under the same general and special provisions, until 31 December 2023, as does the constituent local governments' share of income taxes collected within the region. Infrastructure capital outlays may be obligated to the end of 2023 with construction, inspection and payment running to 30 June 2024; operating expenses and other capital outlays may be obligated to the end of 2023 with delivery, inspection and payment to 31 March 2024. Personnel services, by contrast, stay valid only until 31 December 2022 — salaries do not get extended.

The provision also states what happens at the end. Unreleased appropriations lapse. Unexpended or undisbursed funds revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation under Section 19, Article XII of the Organic Law. Ministries and offices are directed to observe both rules strictly.
readings.whyProposed:
No explanatory note is attached. The structure of the amendment says what happened: a budget written on a cash basis, to be spent within its own year, reached the end of that year with a substantial part of it unspent.

The carve-out for personnel services is the tell that this is about delivery rather than payroll. Salaries were paid; the projects, goods and services were not.
whoIsAffected: Every ministry and office holding unspent 2022 appropriations.
Constituent local government units, whose share of income taxes collected in the region stays available through 2023.
Contractors and suppliers on 2022 procurements, whose delivery and payment windows extend into 2024.
Bangsamoro government employees, who are expressly excluded — personnel services expire on schedule.
The Bangsamoro Treasury, which receives whatever is still unspent when the extension runs out.
implementedBy: Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management (MFBM) — guidelines for implementing the amended cash budgeting provision
Ministries and offices, directed to observe the validity of appropriations and the reversion of funds

funding.detail: No new money. The bill extends the availability of appropriations already made in BAA 23, and expressly does not extend personnel services.

whatChanges: The 2022 regional budget, except salaries, stays spendable through 2023.
Local governments' share of income taxes collected in the region stays disbursable through 2023.
Infrastructure may be completed and paid to 30 June 2024; goods and operating items to 31 March 2024.
Personnel services expire on 31 December 2022 regardless.
Whatever is left after the extension reverts to a Special Fund in the Treasury for reappropriation.
readings.insight:
The reversion clause is the part worth reading closely, because it is the only place in this short bill where the region says what it does with money it could not spend. Unreleased appropriations lapse; unexpended balances go back to the Treasury into a Special Fund, to be reappropriated under Section 19, Article XII of the Organic Law. The exclusion of personnel services is the clearest signal in the sequence. Salaries are spent on time; capital and operating budgets are not. This is also the most populous of the 8, at 36,438, and records the highest barangay income after Pahamudin at about ₱39.5 million.

Eight cabinet bills were filed together in December 2022 to constitute the Special Geographic Areas as municipalities — Bills 129 through 136 — and all 8 became law on 17 August 2023 as BAA 41 through 48. Parliament's bills index records that outcome for Bill No. 136 alone. The other 7, this one among them, are still listed as sitting at Second Reading, Committee Stage, three years after they were enacted.

The plebiscite question is the same across the set and cuts the same way. The vote is held only in the barangays being constituted, so the North Cotabato municipality losing them has no say — which is defensible here in a way it is not elsewhere in the registry, because these barangays had already voted in 2019 to leave that province altogether. What the design does not address is the mother municipality's own position: it loses territory, population and revenue by a regional law it cannot vote on, under a national allotment formula nobody in this Parliament controls.

readings.whatItDoes:
This constitutes the Municipality of Tugunan in the Special Geographic Areas, out of 8 barangays — 7 from Pikit and Tapodoc from Aleosan, both in North Cotabato Pikit and Aleosan, North Cotabato, with its seat of government at Barangay Manaulanan.

The annex is the substance. It lists every constituent barangay with its land area, population and annual income as of 2020, totalling about 102.6 square kilometers, 30,651 residents and roughly ₱37.1 million in combined annual income. The territorial boundary follows the existing barangay lines.

The machinery is identical across all 8. Corporate existence arrives only on ratification by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite in the constituent barangays within 60 days of approval, conducted by COMELEC through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office and charged to COMELEC's own appropriations for the year. The first mayor, vice-mayor and 8 Sangguniang Bayan members are appointed by the Chief Minister and hold office until successors are elected at the next general local elections, while incumbent councillors of the mother municipality who live in the new one serve out their terms there. And because a new municipality has no revenue share until the national allotment reaches it, the Bangsamoro Government must provide not less than ₱2,500,000 every month to run it in the meantime.
readings.whyProposed: Section 2 of every bill in this set carries the fact that explains all of them: these barangays petitioned and voted to be included in the Bangsamoro in the 2019 plebiscite. They chose the region, and then spent years inside it while still administratively attached to a municipality outside it — paying taxes to, and receiving services from, a local government in North Cotabato that they had voted to leave. These bills resolve that anomaly by giving the barangays municipalities of their own.
whoIsAffected: The roughly 30,651 residents of the constituent barangays, who vote on whether the municipality exists.
Pikit and Aleosan, which loses the barangays and does not itself vote.
Incumbent Sangguniang Bayan members of the mother municipality who live in the new one, who finish their terms in the mother municipality.
The Chief Minister, who appoints the entire first municipal government.
COMELEC, which runs the plebiscite and, under this bill, pays for it from its own appropriations.
The Bangsamoro budget, committed to at least ₱2.5 million a month until the revenue allotment arrives.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office — conduct and supervision of the plebiscite
The Chief Minister — appointment of the first mayor, vice-mayor and 8 Sangguniang Bayan members
The Bangsamoro Government — monthly financial assistance pending entitlement to the internal revenue allotment

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 every month for the administration and operation of the new municipal government until it is allocated its share in the internal revenue allotment — at that floor, at least ₱30 million a year, for an unstated period. Against that, the annex records the constituent barangays' own combined annual income at about ₱37.1 million. The plebiscite is charged to COMELEC's available funds under the current fiscal year appropriations.

whatChanges: 8 barangays — 7 from pikit and tapodoc from aleosan, both in north cotabato Pikit and Aleosan, North Cotabato become a municipality of their own inside the Bangsamoro.
Barangays that voted to join the region in 2019 stop being administered from outside it.
The first municipal government is appointed by the Chief Minister rather than elected.
The regional budget takes on a monthly floor of at least ₱2.5 million.
readings.insight:
This bill became BAA 47 on 17 August 2023, keeping its name. The name and the seat both held. The barangay count is the one thing that does not match: this bill lists 8 — 7 from Pikit plus Tapodoc from Aleosan — while the enacted act is recorded as constituting 9 from Pikit and Aleosan. The annexed population is the same 30,651 in both, so if a barangay was added it brought no population with it, and the more likely explanation is a counting difference to be checked against the signed act.

Like Bill No. 131, this measure reaches across a provincial municipality's line to pick up a single barangay — Tapodoc from Aleosan. Those single-barangay additions are what make the Special Geographic Areas awkward to draw: the 2019 vote was taken barangay by barangay, so the resulting territory is not a block of contiguous municipalities but a patchwork that has to be reassembled from pieces of 5 different North Cotabato towns.

Eight cabinet bills were filed together in December 2022 to constitute the Special Geographic Areas as municipalities — Bills 129 through 136 — and all 8 became law on 17 August 2023 as BAA 41 through 48. Parliament's bills index records that outcome for Bill No. 136 alone. The other 7, this one among them, are still listed as sitting at Second Reading, Committee Stage, three years after they were enacted.

The plebiscite question is the same across the set and cuts the same way. The vote is held only in the barangays being constituted, so the North Cotabato municipality losing them has no say — which is defensible here in a way it is not elsewhere in the registry, because these barangays had already voted in 2019 to leave that province altogether. What the design does not address is the mother municipality's own position: it loses territory, population and revenue by a regional law it cannot vote on, under a national allotment formula nobody in this Parliament controls.

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the cabinet bill that became Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 48. It proposes a new municipality, Ligawasan, built from seven barangays of Pikit, North Cotabato — Bagoinged, Barungis, Bulol, Buliok, Gli-Gli, Kabasalan, and Rajamuda — all of which voted in the 2019 plebiscite to join the Bangsamoro and now sit in the region's Special Geographic Areas.

The bill separates those barangays from Pikit and constitutes them as a distinct municipality, with its seat of government at Barangay Bagoinged and a boundary following the existing barangay lines. Annexed tables give the detail: about 112 square kilometers, roughly 29,800 residents, and combined annual income of about ₱31.6 million as of 2020.

The municipality would come into existence only after a plebiscite held within 60 days of approval, conducted by the Commission on Elections through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, and only if a majority of votes cast approve. Until an election, the first mayor, vice-mayor, and council would be appointed.

Because a new municipality gets no share of national revenue immediately, the bill commits the Bangsamoro Government to provide financial assistance of not less than ₱2,500,000 every month for the new local government's administration and operation, until its revenue share is allocated.
readings.whyProposed: The seven barangays voted in 2019 to move from North Cotabato into the Bangsamoro but remained administratively attached to Pikit, a municipality outside the region. The bill invokes the Bangsamoro Government's power to create and alter municipalities and gives those barangays a local government inside the region they voted to join.
whoIsAffected: Roughly 29,800 residents of the seven barangays, across about 112 square kilometers.
The Municipality of Pikit, North Cotabato, which would lose the seven barangays.
Elected officials of Pikit residing in those barangays, whose positions the bill addresses.
The Bangsamoro Government, which would carry at least ₱2.5 million a month until national revenue sharing begins.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections, through the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which would conduct and supervise the plebiscite
The Bangsamoro Government, which would appropriate the monthly assistance
Appointed first municipal officials, pending an election

funding.detail: Not less than ₱2,500,000 per month from the Bangsamoro Government until the new municipality is allocated its share of national revenue. Plebiscite expenses are to be taken from available COMELEC funds under its current appropriation.

whatChanges: Seven barangays leave Pikit and form a municipality, subject to the plebiscite.
A new local government is stood up at Bagoinged, appointed at first.
The Bangsamoro Government takes on a monthly financial commitment with a stated floor.
The region's Special Geographic Areas gain a municipality of their own.
readings.insight: This bill is worth comparing with the act it became. The ₱2.5 million monthly floor written here does not survive into Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 48, which promises monthly assistance without naming an amount. If you want to know what a new municipality in the Special Geographic Areas is actually guaranteed, the answer is in the act, not in this bill — and it is less specific than what was filed.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a Level 1 general hospital in Northern Kabuntalan, Maguindanao del Norte, to be known as the Northern Kabuntalan Municipal Hospital.

The operative text is short and conventional for the genre: a hospital, under the health ministry, funded through the Bangsamoro appropriations. What carries the bill is the explanatory note, and in particular 1 sentence of it about how people actually get to a hospital.

Northern Kabuntalan is a 5th class municipality of around 26,000 residents whose only health facility is a Rural Health Unit limited to checkups, basic treatment and pregnancy deliveries. Anything beyond that — cancer patients needing management, dengue patients needing further treatment, first-time or difficult deliveries, anyone needing monitoring, observation or laboratory testing — is referred out to Midsayap, Libungan or Dalikan, and some go as far as Cotabato City.

The municipality provides an ambulance for selected cases. Most residents travel by habal-habal, the single-motorcycle transport that serves rural Mindanao. Those living on the riverside of Northern Kabuntalan take a boat first and continue by land.
readings.whyProposed:
The note grounds the bill in Section 22, Article IX of the Organic Law — the mandate to establish a general hospital system by law — and in the constitutional duty to make health services available at affordable cost.

Its own argument is narrower and better. A rural health unit that can deliver a straightforward baby and treat a straightforward fever is not a hospital, and the gap between those 2 things is measured here in habal-habal rides and boat crossings. The note also notes the hospital would serve the neighbouring municipalities of Mother Kabuntalan and Datu Piang, so the catchment is wider than the 26,000 the bill is filed for.
whoIsAffected: The roughly 26,000 residents of Northern Kabuntalan, whose only facility handles checkups, basic treatment and deliveries.
Patients needing cancer management, dengue treatment, difficult deliveries, monitoring or laboratory work, all currently referred out of the municipality.
Residents of the riverside barangays, who reach a hospital by boat and then by land.
The neighbouring municipalities of Mother Kabuntalan and Datu Piang, named in the note as likely users.
Hospitals in Midsayap, Libungan, Dalikan and Cotabato City, which carry this catchment now.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health — supervision of the hospital and its organizational structure

funding.detail: The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" but the filed copy names no amount. The enacted act did: BAA 68 appropriates ₱50 million from the Miscellaneous and Personnel Benefit Fund of the 2025 Bangsamoro budget, and separately directs the Ministry to ensure funding for the building, infrastructure, equipment, maintenance and personnel.

whatChanges: Northern Kabuntalan gains a Level 1 hospital where it had a rural health unit.
Referrals out of the municipality — to Midsayap, Libungan, Dalikan or Cotabato City — stop being the only option.
Two neighbouring municipalities gain a nearer facility.
readings.insight:
What Parliament added to this bill is the most interesting devolution scheme in the hospital series. BAA 68 has the Ministry of Health take *full* responsibility for the hospital's financial management at the start — budget allocation, procurement, expenditures — and then transfer it to the municipality in phases, against benchmarks, with the Ministry evaluating whether the local government has shown sufficient capacity, including compliance with accounting standards and efficient procurement.

Set that beside the Basilan pair. Bills 104 and 105 proposed provincial control from day one and the enacted acts reversed them into regional control with a later handover. Here the bill said nothing about who manages the money and the act supplied a staged answer keyed to demonstrated capacity. Across 3 hospitals, Parliament reached the same conclusion each time: the region runs it until the local government can prove it is ready — and, in this one, defined what proof looks like.

The explanatory note is worth keeping for the word habal-habal. Health access papers are usually written in kilometers and travel times; this one names the vehicle, which is a single motorcycle carrying a patient who may be in labour or bleeding, over roads that a 5th class municipality maintains. A bill that says its constituents reach hospital care by motorcycle and boat has made the case more effectively than any statistic in the document.

readings.whatItDoes:
This sets up a Madaris Education Fund Assistance — a fund for private Islamic schools covering infrastructure, scholarships, teacher development and accreditation.

The assistance is awarded against criteria the bill lists: continuous teacher training, infrastructure facilities, scholarship grants, the socio-economic needs of students with priority to the poorest, the school’s overall performance, and the academic qualifications and financial needs of both students and teachers.

What the fund pays for is set out as 10 items: a nutrition and feeding program for young children; classroom facilities down to desks, tables and chalkboards; textbook assistance at a ratio of one book per student per subject; an in-service training fund for teachers; scholarship grants to children of teachers; scholarship grants to qualified students; funding for training and seminars for Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education teachers; an increase in ALIVE teachers’ salaries; funding for madaris registration and accreditation; and madrasah infrastructure development.

MBHTE issues the rules, in coordination with other agencies.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section recognizes the complementary role of private educational institutions and the contribution madaris make to educating the region’s children, and commits to a fund system for their infrastructure, scholarships, teacher development and accreditation, with subsidies aimed particularly at the underprivileged. It also commits the government to encouraging non-formal, informal and indigenous learning systems.

The underlying problem is the same one Bills 167 and 168 address: madaris teach a large share of Bangsamoro children, sit outside the public funding system, and have no standing route to regional money.
whoIsAffected: Madaris across the region, for infrastructure, textbooks, classroom furniture and accreditation costs.
ALIVE teachers — Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education — who would receive training funds and a salary increase.
Teachers in madaris generally, through an in-service training fund and scholarships for their children.
Students, through scholarships, textbooks at one book per subject, and a feeding program for the young ones.
MBHTE’s Bureau of Madaris, which would administer the fund out of its own current appropriation.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education (MBHTE), which issues the rules
MBHTE Bureau of Madaris, against whose current appropriations the fund is charged

funding.detail: ₱10,000,000 for initial implementation, provided in the Bangsamoro Appropriation Act and charged under the current appropriations of the MBHTE Bureau of Madaris. It is one of the few bills in this group to carry a figure at all — and it is a small one against a list of 10 funded items that includes region-wide infrastructure development, one textbook per student per subject, and a salary increase for a whole category of teachers.

whatChanges: A standing fund exists for madaris, covering infrastructure, textbooks, training, scholarships and accreditation.
ALIVE teachers get a training fund and a salary increase.
Textbook assistance is set at a ratio of 1 book per student per subject.
Children of madrasah teachers become eligible for scholarships.
The cost of madaris registration and accreditation is funded.
₱10 million is charged against the Bureau of Madaris’ current appropriations.
readings.insight:
Read this next to Bills 167 and 168 and the picture changes. Three separate bills in this Parliament propose to fund madrasah education: this one from MPs Matalam, Ismael and Alih, Bill 167 from MPs Ampatuan and Mitmug, and Bill 168 from MP Antao. All three were filed within four months of each other in 2023. Bill 167 and this bill overlap substantially — both fund student assistance, teacher support, classroom facilities and textbooks — and their forms of assistance are close enough to read as variations on one draft. Whether they are consolidated is a decision for the committee, and Parliament’s index shows all three sitting in the Committee on Basic, Higher and Technical Education or with Finance alongside it.

The ₱10 million is the number to weigh. It is charged not as new money but against the Bureau of Madaris’ existing appropriations, and it is asked to cover 10 categories including madrasah infrastructure development region-wide and a salary increase for ALIVE teachers. Either the figure is a token first tranche or the list is aspirational; the bill does not say which.

The most concrete thing in it is the textbook ratio. One book per student per subject sounds unremarkable until you have been in a classroom where a book is shared between four children, which in this region is not a rare sight.

readings.whatItDoes:
This directs the Bangsamoro Government to establish orphanages in every province and builds the system around them.

An orphaned minor is defined as a child under 18 left without care or guardian by the death of the father, or without proper parental care through the death, disappearance or abandonment by both parents for at least 6 continuous months.

Section 5 creates a monitoring and evaluating system whose membership reaches from the regional ministry down to the barangay: the Ministry of Social Services and Development, the provincial, municipal and city social welfare offices, the interior ministry, and provincial, local and barangay local government units — and then traditional leaders and the religious sector, the Ulama or Imam of each province. Its job is to identify and select qualified beneficiaries by a transparent and cost-efficient method, to keep updated data on the number, location and personal profile of orphaned minors in each community, to develop the appropriate model of orphanage for that community, and to monitor the children once they are in one.

A Comprehensive Support Program is institutionalised covering 6 named needs: basic needs, physical safety and security, socio-economic needs, educational needs, emotional and spiritual needs, and access to justice. A Managing Committee runs each orphanage and trains its staff, and is responsible for every child admitted until that child turns 18.

Section 10 sets the timetable, and it is the only hard target in the bill: the social services ministry is to begin accreditation immediately, with at least 2 accredited orphanages in every province by the end of the transition period and an accredited orphanage in every local government unit by 2025. The ministry may adopt the national department's accreditation standards or write entirely new ones.

Local governments must monitor the orphanages in their jurisdiction and help them toward accreditation, funded from their own appropriations.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note rests on one finding, from The Asia Foundation's 2020 study *Children of War: A Rapid Needs Assessment of Orphans in Muslim Mindanao*: there are no orphanages or shelters accredited by the national social welfare department anywhere in the Bangsamoro region.

What follows from that is the rest of the case. Muslim orphans processed in Mindanao are often sent to orphanages in Manila, and the facilities that do serve Bangsamoro children have grown up in the diaspora instead — Maharlika Village in Taguig, Culiat in Quezon City, Quiapo, and Baguio City. A region with its own government, emerging from a conflict that produced the orphans in question, was sending them 900 kilometres away to be cared for.
whoIsAffected: Orphaned children under 18 across the region, for whom no accredited facility currently exists.
Children currently sent to orphanages in Manila or cared for in diaspora-run facilities in Taguig, Quezon City, Quiapo and Baguio.
The Ministry of Social Services and Development, which must accredit institutions and may write its own standards.
Every province, required to have at least 2 accredited orphanages by the end of the transition period.
Every local government unit, required to have an accredited orphanage by 2025 and to fund monitoring from its own appropriations.
Traditional leaders and the Ulama or Imam of each province, seated on the monitoring system.
implementedBy: Ministry of Social Services and Development (MSSD) — lead ministry, accreditation, and central planning and monitoring
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government (MILG), coordinating and co-drafting the implementing rules within 3 months
A monitoring and evaluating system seating regional, provincial, municipal, city and barangay bodies together with traditional leaders and the Ulama or Imam of each province
A Managing Committee for each orphanage, responsible for every child until age 18
Constituent local government units, monitoring orphanages in their jurisdiction from their own appropriations

funding.detail: No amount is named. The financial requirements are met through the implementing ministries' appropriations, with local governments funding monitoring and accreditation assistance from their own appropriations. Identical to the funding clause in Bill No. 112.

whatChanges: The region commits to having accredited orphanages of its own rather than sending children to Manila.
At least 2 accredited orphanages per province by the end of the transition period, and 1 per local government unit by 2025.
A single system holds the data on who and where the region's orphaned children are.
Traditional and religious leaders sit in the body that identifies beneficiaries.
Care covers 6 defined needs including emotional and spiritual needs and access to justice.
readings.insight:
This is the clearest case of duplicate legislation in the registry, and it is worth being exact about the evidence rather than calling the 2 bills similar. Normalise both operative texts and they contain the same number of words — 1,255 — and match to better than 95%, with the residual differences traceable to scan noise and page furniture. Seventeen sections, same headings, same order, same definitions, same 2025 deadline, same 6 categories of need.

What that tells you is not that anybody acted improperly. Model bills circulate, civil society organisations draft text and offer it to whoever will file it, and the Asia Foundation study both versions rely on was published for exactly that purpose. Two members filing the same text 3 months apart is what happens when a subject has an obvious champion text and no coordinating mechanism inside Parliament to notice it has already been filed.

The cost of that is visible in the outcome. Both bills went to committee and both stopped. The same thing happened, on a larger scale, to the 8 competing topnotcher and athlete incentive bills — filed within 1 week of each other, referred to the same 2 committees on the same day 16 months later, none enacted. Duplication does not merely waste drafting effort; it splits the sponsorship of a subject so that no single measure carries the weight of a member's reputation, and committees receive 2 identical papers instead of 1 with 2 names on it.

The substance deserves better than that. The finding underneath both bills — that the region had no accredited orphanage and sent its orphans to Manila — is among the sharpest facts in the registry, and the deadline both bills set for fixing it has now passed.

Bill No. 112 and Bill No. 143 are the same bill. Both carry the title "An Act Institutionalizing Support to the Welfare and Care for Orphans by Establishing Bangsamoro Orphanages", both run to 17 sections with identical headings in identical order, and set side by side the operative texts run to 1,255 words each and match almost word for word — the few differences being scan artefacts rather than drafting. MP Ramos filed hers on 17 October 2022; MP Anayatin filed the same text on 17 January 2023, 3 months later. Both were referred to committee and both are still there.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates the Bangsamoro Convention Center as a government-owned and controlled corporation with its own legal personality, and puts it in the Municipality of Parang, Maguindanao del Norte.

The Center is to host local and international conventions, meetings, fairs and social events, and to provide the facilities for them — the text names meeting rooms, exhibition halls, auditoriums and accommodation. It may set and collect its own fees and charges, enter contracts, market itself, and form partnerships with private and public entities.

It is run by a board of trustees chaired by the Chief Minister, sitting with the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism, the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the Chairman of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Governor of Maguindanao del Norte, and two private sector representatives appointed by the Chief Minister. The board sets policy and appoints a chief executive officer for day-to-day operations, and must issue implementing rules within 60 days. The Center reports annually to the Bangsamoro Government and the relevant committees of Parliament, and is subject to audit.
readings.whyProposed: The declaration of policy is the whole argument: to provide a venue for local and international conventions, meetings, fairs and social events in order to promote economic growth and cultural exchange, and to establish the Bangsamoro as a leading destination for events and gatherings. The region currently has no purpose-built facility at that scale, and hosts its larger gatherings in hotel function rooms, university halls and government buildings.
whoIsAffected: The Municipality of Parang and Maguindanao del Norte, which would host the facility and whose Governor sits on its board.
The regional events, tourism and hospitality trade, which gains a venue and a competitor at the same time.
The Bangsamoro Government, which would carry the cost of building and standing up a corporation.
Organizers of regional gatherings, who currently work around the absence of a large purpose-built venue.
implementedBy: The Bangsamoro Convention Center, as a government-owned and controlled corporation under the management and supervision of the Bangsamoro Government

A board of trustees chaired by the Chief Minister, with the Ministers of Trade, Investments and Tourism and of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, the Chairman of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Governor of Maguindanao del Norte, and two private sector appointees
A chief executive officer appointed by the board

funding.detail: No figure appears anywhere in the bill. The amount necessary for initial implementation is to be included in the annual general appropriations act, and the Center is expected to generate funds of its own through fees, charges and partnerships. For a measure whose entire purpose is to build a building, the absence of any construction estimate is the most conspicuous thing in the text.

whatChanges: A Bangsamoro Convention Center exists as a corporation with its own legal personality.
It is sited at Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, rather than at the seat of government.
It can set and keep its own fees and charges and enter its own contracts and partnerships.
The Chief Minister chairs its board and appoints two private sector trustees.
It reports annually to Parliament’s relevant committees and is subject to audit.
readings.insight:
The siting is the decision worth arguing about, and the bill does not argue it. Parang is not the seat of government — Cotabato City is, half an hour away — but Parang holds Polloc port and the region’s freeport, and putting a convention center next to a deepwater harbour rather than next to the ministries is a bet on trade traffic over government traffic. The text states the location in a single clause and gives no reasoning for it.

The second thing is the board. Four of its seven seats are held ex officio by the Chief Minister and ministers, one by a provincial governor, and two by private sector appointees the Chief Minister chooses. A corporation meant to compete for international events is governed almost entirely by people whose day job is something else, and the trade it serves has no seat that is not in the Chief Minister’s gift.

Third, and most practically: the bill authorises a corporation to build and run a convention center and never says what that costs. Every other creation measure of this size in the registry carries at least an initial figure. This one leaves the whole question to the annual appropriations act, which means the decision that matters — how big, and how much — is made after the law rather than in it.

It has moved further than most. The index has it at Second Reading, deferred in July and again in August 2025, which puts it among the handful of bills in this batch past the committee stage.
