readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes 1 dialysis centre, at the Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital in Pinaring, Sultan Kudarat, and it is the only 1 of the 3 dialysis bills that says how it will be paid for.

Section 10 appropriates ₱20,000,000 for the facilities, equipment, machines and supplies needed to open. The hospital provides the building and the space and hires or designates the physicians, nurses and administrative staff, charged against its own budget. All purchased equipment is owned and maintained by the hospital, with deeds of transfer executed as needed.

The pricing rule is the distinctive provision. Section 7 caps the service fee at no more than 110% of the supplier's cost per treatment, and charges nothing at all to indigent patients. Section 8 then lets the collections accrue to the centre's own income, to be used primarily for its operation — so the 10% margin above supplier cost is what funds the centre's running expenses.

Section 9 adds bridging support: the Ministry of Health, through its Ayudang Medikal mula sa Bangsamoro Government programme, allocates funds to augment the centre's expenses during its first year.

A Joint Technical Working Group of the health ministry and the hospital writes the implementing rules, covering hiring, procurement, construction under the national Department of Health's administrative orders, and the centre's licensing and regulation.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note gives a figure rather than a principle. Renal disease is among the major causes of disease-related death in the country, and at Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital alone there were 162 patients in 2022 needing dialysis.

That is the argument: a specific hospital, a counted caseload, and a facility sized to it. The bill does not claim to solve the region's kidney disease problem; it claims that 162 patients at 1 hospital justify a centre there.
whoIsAffected: The 162 patients the note counts at Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital in 2022, and those who follow them.
Indigent patients, who pay no service fee at all.
Paying patients, whose fee is capped at 110% of the supplier's cost per treatment.
Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital, which provides the building, hires the staff from its own budget and owns the equipment.
The Ministry of Health, which augments the first year through its AMBaG medical assistance programme.
implementedBy: Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital — building, space, staffing, ownership and maintenance of equipment
Ministry of Health, through the Ayudang Medikal mula sa Bangsamoro Government (AMBaG) Programme, for first-year assistance
A Joint Technical Working Group of the Ministry of Health and the hospital, writing the implementing rules

funding.detail: ₱20,000,000 appropriated for facilities, equipment, machines and supplies for initial operation. The building, space and staff costs fall on the hospital's own budget. Thereafter the centre funds itself: fees capped at 110% of the supplier's cost per treatment accrue to the centre as income and pay primarily for its operation, with free treatment for indigents and first-year augmentation from the health ministry's AMBaG programme.

whatChanges: A dialysis centre opens at Cotabato Sanitarium and General Hospital with ₱20 million of equipment.
Dialysis is free for indigent patients and capped at 110% of supplier cost for everyone else.
The centre keeps its own fee income and runs on it.
The health ministry's medical assistance programme covers the first year's shortfall.
readings.insight:
The 110% cap is the most interesting mechanism in any of the 3 dialysis bills, and it is doing 2 jobs at once. It protects the patient — a session cannot be priced at more than a tenth above what the consumables actually cost, which forecloses the margins that make private dialysis unaffordable. And because Section 8 lets the collections stay with the centre, that same 10% is the centre's operating budget. It is a self-financing design, and its weakness is visible on the face of it: 10% of consumable cost will not cover staff, maintenance and machine replacement, which is presumably why the hospital carries the salaries and the health ministry has to bridge year one.

The bill's real virtue is that it is the only 1 of the 3 that is costed and therefore buildable. Bill No. 88 requires a unit in every government hospital in the region and funds it from "current appropriations"; Bill No. 279 requires one in every provincial tertiary hospital within a year and does the same. This bill names ₱20 million, names the hospital, names who owns the equipment afterwards and names the programme that covers the first year. A single facility that opens is worth more to a patient than a regional mandate that does not.

The counted caseload is the other thing to credit. "162 patients for the year 2022" at a named hospital is the kind of number almost no bill in this registry supplies, and it makes the measure checkable — a reader can ask whether a centre sized for 162 patients is enough, which is a question the other 2 bills give no way of asking.

What the bill does not address is everyone outside Sultan Kudarat. A dialysis patient needs treatment 2 or 3 times a week for life, so a centre serves only the people who can reach it that often. For Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, a facility at Pinaring is not a service, and the island provinces are exactly where Bill 88's regionwide mandate was aimed.

Three bills in this registry address dialysis and they pick 3 different scales. Bill No. 88, filed by MP Mawallil in October 2022, requires a dialysis unit in every government hospital in the region within 5 years. Bill No. 145, filed by MP Sema in February 2023, builds 1 centre at 1 named hospital with ₱20 million behind it. Bill No. 279, filed by MP Dilangalen in February 2024, requires provincial tertiary hospitals to have a unit within 1 year. All 3 are at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and none has become law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 145, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This upgrades the Datu Odin Sinsuat District Hospital from 50 beds to 100, with its facilities and professional complement raised with it.

The bill's real subject is a gap between 2 laws and a building. Republic Act No. 11330 converted the facility into a 50-bed district hospital; the note says the funds released to it have remained at the level of a 10-bed budget since that adoption, and the hospital's physical structure was built for Level I status at 10 beds. So the 50-bed designation exists on paper, the money is for 10 beds, and the building is for 10 beds.
readings.whyProposed:
The note's argument is about implementation rather than need. A national statute gave the hospital a 50-bed designation and neither the budget nor the building followed, so the institution has spent years carrying a status it was never resourced to hold.

Asking for 100 beds in that context is asking for the whole thing to be done properly once — a structure, a budget and a staffing complement matched to a designation — rather than for a second unfunded upgrade on top of the first.
whoIsAffected: Patients of Datu Odin Sinsuat, the largest municipality in Maguindanao del Norte by population.
The hospital's staff, working in a building designed for a 10-bed Level I facility.
Anyone relying on a hospital whose funding has remained at 10-bed levels despite a 50-bed designation.
The Ministry of Health and the finance ministry, which would have to fund the structure as well as the beds.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital, approve its structure and staffing, and fund its facilities

funding.detail: No amount is named. The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act. Comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of size.

whatChanges: A 50-bed designation that was never funded becomes a 100-bed hospital with the budget and building to match.
The facility's physical structure is upgraded beyond the Level I, 10-bed design it was built to.
Professional and medical staffing rises with the capacity.
readings.insight:
This is the only hospital bill in the registry whose complaint is that an existing law was never implemented, and that makes it the most useful of the set for understanding why the others may not work either. Republic Act No. 11330 designated this hospital at 50 beds. The designation arrived; the construction budget did not, and the operating budget stayed at the 10-bed level. A decade of bills in this registry create and upgrade hospitals by statute on the assumption that the designation is the hard part — this one is evidence that it is the easy part.

Read against the enacted acts, the pattern holds. BAA 73 converted the Iranun District Hospital to 200 beds with ₱50 million; BAA 74 made the Maguindanao Provincial Hospital a 350-bed Level III facility with the same ₱50 million. Those figures buy neither a building nor a staff at that scale, which is precisely the position this bill describes Datu Odin Sinsuat as already being in.

Asking for 100 beds when the funded reality is 10 is therefore a calculated move rather than an overreach. The bill is not requesting a doubling of an operating 50-bed hospital; it is requesting that a facility be built and funded for the first time, and choosing a number that reflects the municipality's size rather than the paper status it already has. Whether Parliament reads it that way is the question, and the registry's habit of converging on smaller figures suggests the risk.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 146, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes: This establishes and constructs a Level I municipal hospital with 50 beds in Datu Piang, Maguindanao del Sur, to be known as the Datu Piang Municipal Hospital, appropriating funds for its facilities and professional health care and medical personnel.
readings.whyProposed:
Datu Piang had a population of 28,380 at the 2020 census and no hospital of its own.

The measure is 1 of 2 hospital bills MP Anayatin filed on the same day — the other upgrades the Datu Odin Sinsuat District Hospital — and both are framed around the same problem: a municipality's population measured against provision that does not exist or was never funded.
whoIsAffected: The 28,380 residents of Datu Piang recorded at the 2020 census.
Patients currently travelling out of the municipality for any hospital care.
Neighbouring facilities that absorb the catchment.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the new hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital, approve its structure and staffing, and fund its facilities

funding.detail: No amount is named. The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act. Comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of size.

whatChanges: Datu Piang gains a 50-bed Level I municipal hospital.
Funds are appropriated for facilities and for professional and medical personnel, not only for the building.
A municipality of over 28,000 stops depending on hospitals elsewhere.
readings.insight:
Fifty beds for 28,380 people is nearly twice the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000 that other bills in this registry invoke, and the bill does not explain the margin. There are defensible reasons — Datu Piang sits in the Liguasan marsh area, among the most flood-prone and historically conflict-affected parts of the region, where a hospital serves a wider catchment than its own municipality in an emergency — but the note does not make that argument, and a committee comparing this bill against the Ambolodto measures, which size hospitals precisely to population, would have to supply it.

The title's specificity about what the money is for is the bill's better feature. It appropriates funds "for its facilities and professional health care, medical personnel" rather than simply for the hospital. Nearly every hospital measure in this registry funds a building and leaves the staffing to be found inside an existing ministry line, and the companion bill by the same author documents exactly what that produces: a 50-bed designation running on a 10-bed budget for years. Naming personnel in the appropriation is the lesson of that experience written into the next bill.

Datu Piang is also the mother municipality of several units created in this registry's own pages, including barangays that appear in the parliamentary districts schedule. A hospital there serves a population that has been administratively rearranged more than once, and the bill's decision to size it above the municipality's own count reads better against that than against a ratio.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 147, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a BARMM Badjao Development Project, and it is the only measure in the registry addressed to a single ethnic community.

Section 2 states the premise without hedging: the Badjao community is "arguably the most marginalized, disenfranchised, vulnerable, disadvantaged and isolated indigenous ethnic group in the region and falling behind all human development indicators, at individual, familial and communal levels". The policy covers their basic political and human rights — including birth and citizenship registration — and the promotion and protection of their marine ecology and lifestyle.

The project is built on the United Nations Human Security framework, and its 7 objectives follow that framework's categories. Political security: supporting ancestral domain claims and the establishment of their own kampung, and ensuring participation in BARMM decision-making. Economic security: livelihoods in fishing, agriculture and handicrafts, support for traditional economic practices, and a route into the global creative economy and eco- and cultural tourism. Food security, including support for traditional food practices. Health security, including traditional health practices. Environmental security: protecting their marine ecology and lifestyle, and awarding ancestral domain claims "where they can begin communal life anew". Personal security: education, housing, cultural identity and heritage. And community security: social cohesion, disaster preparedness, and representation in local legislative bodies through the Indigenous People's Mandatory Representation system and in bodies requiring civil society participation.

Section 3 names what the kampung is to be protected from: commercial fishery encroachment, high sea robbery and similar insecurities.

A Project Management Office under the Office of the Chief Minister implements it, with Community Development Officers assigned to clusters of Badjao communities as focal person, facilitator, organizer and conduit, and Provincial Supervisors above them doing quality assurance. A Project Consultative Body of Badjao male and female elders and youth leaders convenes before each annual budget cycle to give inputs on policies and programmes affecting them.
readings.whyProposed:
Birth and citizenship registration appearing in the declaration of policy is the tell. The Badjao are a seafaring people whose communities live on boats and in stilt villages across the Sulu archipelago and whose members frequently hold no birth certificate — which means no school enrolment, no PhilHealth, no bank account, no passport and, in the most serious cases, no demonstrable citizenship in any of the 3 countries whose waters they move through.

The bill's answer is to treat that as a security problem rather than a welfare one, which is why it reaches for the Human Security framework. A community that can be moved off a shoreline, fished out by commercial fleets, robbed at sea and left undocumented is insecure in several distinct ways at once, and the framework gives the bill a way to name all 7 of them in a single programme.
whoIsAffected: The Badjao communities of the region, including those living on boats and in stilt settlements.
Badjao without birth or citizenship registration, for whom the bill makes documentation a policy objective.
Badjao fishing households competing with commercial fishery encroachment.
Badjao elders and youth leaders, male and female, seated on the Project Consultative Body before each budget cycle.
Local legislative councils, which would seat Badjao representation through the Indigenous People's Mandatory Representation system.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which would house the Project Management Office.
implementedBy: A Project Management Office under the Office of the Chief Minister — supervision, implementation, resource mobilisation and the implementing rules
A Project Consultative Body of Badjao male and female elders and youth leaders, convening before each annual budget cycle
Community Development Officers assigned to clusters of Badjao communities
Provincial Supervisors, serving as quality assurance and compliance officers

funding.detail: No amount is named. The cost is charged against the BARMM budget for the year, and the government may accept donations or grants from external sources. For a programme spanning documentation, livelihoods, housing, health and ancestral domain claims across scattered communities, the absence of a figure is the bill's main structural weakness.

whatChanges: The Badjao become the subject of a dedicated government programme rather than a line in a general one.
Birth and citizenship registration becomes a stated objective of regional policy.
Ancestral domain claims extend to a seafaring people and their kampung.
Commercial fishery encroachment and high sea robbery are named as threats the state will act against.
Badjao elders and youth advise on the budget before it is drafted, not after.
Community Development Officers are placed with clusters of Badjao communities.
readings.insight:
Putting birth registration in a development statute is the most consequential thing this bill does, and it is easy to read past because it sounds administrative. A person with no birth certificate cannot enrol in school, hold a formal job, open an account, claim health insurance or prove citizenship — so every other objective in the bill, from livelihoods to education to housing, is gated behind a document many Badjao do not have. A programme that funds boats and training without fixing registration would reach the people who are already least excluded.

The Human Security framework earns its place here rather than decorating the bill. Most measures in this registry pick 1 instrument — a facility, a subsidy, an office. The Badjao's situation is simultaneously about land they have no title to, seas being fished by others, robbery they cannot report, documents they do not hold and representation they do not have, and a framework with 7 named dimensions is a way of holding all of that in one programme without pretending any single intervention solves it.

The consultative body's timing is the detail that shows real drafting care. It convenes "before the onset of the annual budget cycle" — not after the budget is drafted, when consultation is ratification, but before, when inputs can still shape allocations. Several bodies created elsewhere in this registry are required to consult and none of them says when.

What the bill cannot resolve is its relationship to the enacted indigenous peoples act. BAA 64 brought the Badjao and the Sama peoples expressly within the coverage of the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the ancestral domain machinery, which is most of what this bill's political and environmental security objectives were reaching for. This measure would sit alongside that as a dedicated programme with its own office and field staff, and the case for it after BAA 64 is the gap between having rights recognised in a statute and having a community development officer in the kampung — which, on the bill's own account of where the Badjao stand on every human development indicator, is a real gap.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 148, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a Level I general hospital with 50 beds in Talipao, Sulu.

Talipao is a 1st class rural municipality in Sulu's first district — 52 barangays and a population of 100,088 — and it is among the largest municipalities in the province. It is reachable from the nearest major city, Zamboanga, only by sea or air.

The municipality has no hospital. Its only health facilities are barangay health stations and rural health units.
readings.whyProposed:
The note sets out 2 arguments and the first is historical. In the 1970s, at the height of the war between the MNLF and the Armed Forces, and again during the more recent fighting with the Abu Sayyaf, Talipao was among the most brutally affected areas, enduring tremendous human suffering and loss of life and property.

The second is the referral chain as it now stands. Patients needing emergency care travel to Jolo; and the note is candid that Jolo is not the answer either — the Sulu Provincial Hospital cannot sufficiently provide for severe conditions, so patients continue to Zamboanga City. The note attributes a high mortality rate in the municipality to the absence of healthcare facilities.
whoIsAffected: The 100,088 residents of Talipao across 52 barangays, who have no hospital.
Emergency patients travelling first to Jolo and then, if necessary, to Zamboanga City.
Communities that bore the heaviest fighting in the 1970s and again more recently.
The Sulu Provincial Hospital in Jolo, which the note says cannot sufficiently handle severe cases.
The Ministry of Health, which would establish and supervise the hospital.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the figure is left to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: A municipality of over 100,000 people gains its first hospital.
Barangay health stations and rural health units stop being the only provision for 52 barangays.
The referral chain to Jolo and onward to Zamboanga City stops being the only option.
readings.insight:
One hundred thousand people and no hospital is the plainest statement of need in this registry. Talipao is larger than several municipalities for which the region has enacted hospital acts — South Ubian has about 29,500 people and received a 25-bed Level I hospital under BAA 66 — and it has 52 barangays, which is more than 1 of the Special Geographic Area municipalities created in 2023. The bill asks for 50 beds, which on the Department of Health ratio its companion bills invoke is exactly half what the municipality's population implies.

The note's admission about Jolo is what distinguishes it. Most hospital bills in this registry argue that patients must travel to a provincial hospital; this one says the provincial hospital cannot handle severe cases either, so the real destination is Zamboanga City — across water, in another region. That makes the measure about more than convenience: a province of a million people whose referral endpoint is outside it does not have a hospital system, which is the conclusion Bill No. 161's bed arithmetic reaches from the other direction.

The conflict history is included for a reason the bill leaves implicit. A municipality that absorbed heavy fighting in the 1970s and again recently has a population with untreated injury, displacement and the chronic conditions that follow both — and it is precisely the sort of place from which health infrastructure withdraws during a conflict and does not return. Read with MP Alamia's health care subsidy bill, which would give conflict-affected people a card entitling them to subsidised care, the 2 measures address the same population from opposite ends: 1 funds the patient, this one builds the place to treat them.

Sulu's arithmetic is set out in Bill No. 161 and it frames all 4 of the province's hospital bills in this registry. The province has 1,000,108 people and 320 hospital beds. On the Department of Health's own standard — Administrative Order 2006-0004, 1 bed per 1,000 population — that is a shortfall of 680 beds, and even counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the new Maimbung District Hospital, 480 are still missing.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 149, copy as filed, with explanatory note
Parliament Bill No. 151, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires a special help desk for senior citizens and persons with disabilities in every government office and every local government unit in the region.

The desk is where a senior citizen or a person with a disability may make inquiries, ask for assistance and lodge complaints, and it must attend to and address what is brought to it. The bill defines both groups by reference to national law — Republic Act 9994 for senior citizens, any resident citizen at least 60 years old, and Republic Act 10754 for persons with disabilities, using the long-term impairment and barriers formulation.

Section 5 puts the duty on local chief executives by name. Provincial governors, city and municipal mayors must fill the gap in protecting and overseeing the welfare of senior citizens and persons with disabilities in their areas, and all local governments must advocate their rights and take a proactive stance in disseminating information about the benefits and privileges they are entitled to.

The implementing rules are for MSSD to prepare in consultation with MILG within 60 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section is about dignity and access: valuing the dignity of senior citizens and persons with disabilities, guaranteeing full respect for their human rights, and integrating them into mainstream society through programs that ensure easy access to government services.

The practical problem is that the benefits already exist under national law and the barrier is the counter. A person who cannot find out where to go, or who is sent between offices, does not receive an entitlement they legally hold.
whoIsAffected: Senior citizens and persons with disabilities across the region, who gain a named point of contact in every government office.
Every government office and local government unit in BARMM, each of which must staff a desk.
Provincial governors and city and municipal mayors, on whom Section 5 places the duty by name.
MSSD and MILG, which write the implementing rules.
implementedBy: All government offices and local government units in the Bangsamoro, which host the desks
Provincial governors, city and municipal mayors
Ministry of Social Services and Development, with the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, for the implementing rules

funding.detail: No figure. Funds for establishing the desks in all government offices and LGUs are to be included in the annual appropriations of the region and submitted to Parliament for approval. A desk in every office in the region is mostly a staffing cost, and the bill does not estimate it or say whether existing personnel are to be redesignated.

whatChanges: Every government office and LGU in the region must run a special help desk for senior citizens and persons with disabilities.
The desk handles inquiries, assistance and complaints.
Local chief executives carry a named duty to oversee the welfare of both groups.
Local governments must proactively publicise the benefits and privileges available.
MSSD and MILG must issue implementing rules within 60 days.
readings.insight:
This is a small bill and it is aimed at the right thing. Senior citizen and PWD benefits in the Philippines are generous on paper and unevenly delivered in practice, and the failure is almost always at the counter rather than in the statute. A named desk with a duty to take complaints is a cheap intervention against exactly that failure.

What it lacks is a consequence. There is no penalty, no reporting requirement, no obligation to record what the desk receives, and no one designated to check that the desks exist. A duty to establish a desk, with nobody counting them, is likely to produce a sign on a wall in the offices that were already helpful and nothing at all in the ones that were not. A single annual report from MSSD on how many desks are operating and what they handled would change the character of the bill entirely.

The drafting also leaves the desks unstaffed in the literal sense: the Act says a desk is established, not who sits at it. In a small municipal office that will mean a person already doing something else, which is workable — but it should be said, because the appropriation is meant to pay for it.

On its progress: filed February 2023, First Reading May 2023, and referred in July 2025 to three committees at once — Social Services, Women Youth Children and PWDs, and Finance.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 153, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
The Bangsamoro Free Lunch Act of 2023 institutionalises a free lunch for students in public schools, served five days a week for the whole school year, beginning when classes open.

Schools in three situations are given priority: those with reported severe malnutrition, those in areas of armed conflict, and those in highly congested areas.

A Bangsamoro Free Lunch Council supervises. It is chaired by the Minister of Basic, Higher and Technical Education with the Minister of Health as co-chair, and seats the Ministers of Social Services and Development, of Agriculture, and of the Interior and Local Government. The Council writes the framework that serves as the blueprint — the integrated package of nutrition services, an information database, and the operational detail. MBHTE has primary responsibility for administering the program, working to nutritional standards the Act requires, and a School Lunch Committee operates at school level with duties set out for its members.

The program reports annually to Parliament.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section runs from the right to health and access to essential goods and social services to the specific problem of malnutrition among students, and frames the program as protection for children who by reason of their family’s economic circumstances do not get the nutrition their development requires.

The objectives put the educational case alongside the health one: a child who has not eaten does not learn, so mitigating malnourishment is presented as support for the learning process rather than as welfare attached to a school.
whoIsAffected: Students in public schools across the region, who would receive one free meal on every school day.
Schools in areas of severe malnutrition, armed conflict and congestion, given explicit priority.
Families, for whom a guaranteed school meal is a real reduction in household food cost.
MBHTE, which administers the program, and the four other ministries on the Council.
Local suppliers and producers, through a program feeding public school students five days a week — the Minister of Agriculture sits on the Council.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Free Lunch Council — MBHTE as chair, Health as co-chair, with Social Services and Development, Agriculture, and the Interior and Local Government
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, with primary responsibility for administration
School Lunch Committees at school level

funding.detail: No figure. Funds are to be included in the annual General Appropriations of the Bangsamoro and submitted to Parliament for approval. This is the most expensive recurring commitment in this group of bills by a wide margin — a hot meal for every public school student in the region, five days a week, every week of the school year — and it is the one where the absence of a costing is hardest to defend.

whatChanges: Public school students receive one free lunch on every school day of the year.
The meal is served 5 days a week for the full duration of the school year.
Schools with severe malnutrition, in armed conflict areas, or in congested areas are prioritized.
A five-minister Council supervises and writes the nutrition framework.
Each school runs a School Lunch Committee.
The program reports to Parliament annually.
readings.insight:
The coverage does not match itself, and a committee needs to fix it before anything else. Section 3 institutionalises the program "in all kindergarten and elementary students enrolled in all public schools". Section 11 says the Act covers all public schools in the region and every eligible student enrolled, then defines public schools as "primary and secondary educational institutions". So one section limits the program to kindergarten and elementary, and the other pulls in secondary. The difference is a very large number of students and a very large amount of money.

That matters because the bill carries no figure at all. A daily hot meal for every public school student in BARMM is among the largest recurring programs the region could adopt, and whether it covers elementary only or elementary and secondary changes the cost by a multiple. Leaving both the scope and the price to be settled later leaves nothing to scrutinise.

The Minister of Agriculture’s seat on the Council is the quiet good idea. A guaranteed daily purchase of food for every public school in the region is agricultural demand as much as it is nutrition policy, and putting agriculture on the supervising body is how a feeding program becomes a market for local producers rather than a procurement contract.

The priority list is well chosen and worth noting for what it names: schools in areas of armed conflict, alongside malnutrition and congestion. Few feeding bills anywhere would need that category.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates a Lake Lanao Rehabilitation and Development Authority as a body attached to the Office of the Chief Minister, responsible for the overall policy-making, planning, coordination and management of the lake's rehabilitation and development, with regulatory and supervisory authority over programs and projects in the Lake Lanao area.

The board is assembled at the top of government. A Chairman appointed by the Chief Minister chairs it; the Minister of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy is Co-Chair; and the Ministers of Agriculture, Public Works, Trade, Transportation, and Finance sit as members, alongside the Director General of the Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, a representative of the Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur, and 2 representatives of non-government organisations appointed by the Chief Minister from nominations.

The instrument at the centre of the Act is a 30-year Master Plan, and Section 16 specifies what it must contain: an assessment of the physical and natural resources and potential of the Lake Lanao area, its social and economic conditions, hydrological characteristics and power potential; the development of scenic and tourist spots and conservation of water resources; and proposed rehabilitation projects including watershed protection and management, flood control, the revival and restoration of the lake's biodiversity, maintenance of desirable water quality, and socio-economic projects using local raw materials. Everything from provincial to local level must be anchored on that plan, and it must be reviewed regularly against its targets.

Section 18 requires an independent review every 10 years by a panel of experts appointed by the Chief Minister, reporting to the Chief Minister and to Parliament. Section 20 provides that any doubt in interpreting the Act is to be construed liberally in favour of fulfilling its objectives.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill argues from the ecology, with footnotes — to the Australian Museum on biodiversity and to WWF on ecological balance — and from the physical fact that Lake Lanao drains through only one outlet, the Agus River in Lanao del Norte.

That single outlet is why the lake is both ecologically fragile and economically valuable, and the bill's answer is a plan rather than a prohibition: a 30-year horizon covering water quality, biodiversity, watershed, flood control and the livelihoods that depend on all of them, with everything else required to align to it.

The bill also records where it came from. A footnote on its first page states that it was inspired by the entry of Najib A. Haron in the Online Bill and Resolution Drafting Contest run by the offices of MP Ampatuan and MP Mitmug, under the title "An Act Creating Lake Lanao Rehabilitation Program to Preserve, Beautify, Improve, Restore and Utilize the like for Socio-Economic Purposes".
whoIsAffected: Communities in the Lake Lanao area, whose local programs must align with the Master Plan.
The Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur, which holds 1 seat on a board of 10.
Non-government organisations, which hold 2 board seats filled by the Chief Minister from nominations.
Seven ministries whose ministers sit on the board in person.
Fisherfolk and shoreline residents, as the intended beneficiaries of biodiversity revival and water quality provisions.
Parliament, which receives an independent expert review of the Authority every 10 years.
implementedBy: Lake Lanao Rehabilitation and Development Authority, attached to the Office of the Chief Minister

An LLRDA Board of 10 — a Chairman appointed by the Chief Minister, the environment Minister as Co-Chair, 5 further ministers, the planning authority's Director General, a provincial government representative and 2 NGO representatives
An Executive Office under the Board, with the LLRDA Board writing the implementing rules
An independent review panel of experts appointed by the Chief Minister every 10 years, reporting to the Chief Minister and Parliament

funding.detail: No amount is named. Initial operations are charged against the Contingent Fund of the 2023 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, and annual expenditures including capital outlays go into the Bangsamoro appropriations act thereafter. The bill gives the Authority no revenue-raising power of its own.

whatChanges: Lake Lanao gains a single body responsible for its rehabilitation, chaired at cabinet level.
A 30-year Master Plan becomes the instrument every program in the lake area must align to.
Non-government organisations hold seats on the governing board.
An independent expert panel reviews the Authority every decade and reports to Parliament.
Doubts about the Act are resolved in favour of its objectives rather than narrowly.
readings.insight:
The 30-year Master Plan is this bill's real instrument, and it is a better fit for the problem than a regulatory body alone would be. Lake Lanao's difficulties — siltation, water quality, biodiversity loss, a shoreline that moves with the drawdown — are cumulative and slow, and none of them is solved inside a political term. Writing a 30-year horizon into the statute, requiring provincial and local activity to anchor on it, and specifying its contents down to hydrological characteristics and power potential, commits successive governments to a single document rather than to a sequence of projects.

What the bill conspicuously does not do is name the National Power Corporation. The Agus River appears once, as the lake's single outlet; the Master Plan must assess the lake's "power potentials"; and the entity that actually operates the hydroelectric complex on that outlet has no seat, no obligation and no mention. Bill No. 111, covering the same lake, seats NAPOCOR on its board. A plan that assesses power potential without binding the power operator is a plan that can be written and then contradicted by the drawdown, and this is the gap a committee comparing the 2 bills would have to close.

The board composition is the other half of the comparison. Seven ministers in person, a chair appointed by the Chief Minister and 2 NGO seats is a heavyweight regional body — it can requisition attention across government in a way Bill 111's board of provincial directors cannot. The cost is distance: 1 seat for the Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur, no seat for Marawi City, none for the municipal or barangay leagues, and no consultative assembly. The lake is governed for the province rather than by it.

The independent review in Section 18 is the provision most worth keeping from either bill. A panel of experts, appointed outside the Authority, reviewing its policies and programs every 10 years and reporting to Parliament as well as the Chief Minister, is the only external check on a 30-year plan in either document — and 30 years is 3 of those reviews, which is roughly the right cadence for a body whose results cannot be judged in less.

One thing about this bill's provenance deserves recording, because it is rare. The measure began as a citizen's entry in a drafting contest and says so on its own first page, naming the entrant. Three bills in this registry carry that footnote — this one, the Halal Food Certification bill and the bill on the safety and welfare of minors — all traceable to contests run by MP Ampatuan's office with MP Mawallil and MP Mitmug. A parliament that takes legislative text from the public and credits the author by name in the filed copy is doing something most legislatures do not, and the practice is visible only in the footnotes.

Two bills in this registry create an authority for Lake Lanao and they are not versions of each other. Bill No. 111, filed by MP Ramos in October 2022, creates a Ranaw Development Authority run by provincial officials and covering the whole of Lanao del Sur. Bill No. 155, filed by MP Ampatuan in March 2023, creates a Lake Lanao Rehabilitation and Development Authority run by ministers and confined to the lake area. Both are still at Second Reading, Committee Stage. Neither has become law, and the lake has no authority of any kind.

readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes and constructs a Level I municipal hospital with 50 beds in Talayan, Maguindanao, to be known as the Talayan Municipal Hospital, appropriating funds for its facilities, professional health care and medical personnel.

Its declaration of policy carries the wider formulation used in a handful of the region's hospital measures: beyond comprehensive and integrated health service delivery and the basic right to life, the Bangsamoro Government is to act "in order to adequately respond to emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases".
readings.whyProposed:
The bill is short and its case rests on the absence of a facility in the municipality rather than on a documented caseload.

The emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases clause is the one substantive addition to the standard policy language, and it is the same sentence that appears in the Masiu hospital bill which became BAA 69 — drafted in the years after both the Marawi siege and the pandemic, in a province where displacement and flooding are recurrent.
whoIsAffected: The residents of Talayan, Maguindanao, who have no hospital in the municipality.
Patients travelling to facilities in neighbouring municipalities.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital.
Communities affected by flooding and displacement, addressed through the emergencies and disasters clause.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital, approve its structure and staffing, and fund its facilities

funding.detail: No amount is named. The title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act. Comparable hospitals enacted in this registry each received ₱50 million initially, regardless of size.

whatChanges: Talayan gains a 50-bed Level I municipal hospital.
Funds are appropriated for personnel as well as facilities.
The hospital's mandate expressly covers emergencies, disasters and emerging diseases.
readings.insight:
This is the thinnest of the hospital bills on evidence and it is worth saying so. Where the Ambolodto measures compute a bed deficiency from census data and a published ratio, and the South Upi bill cites 5 years of occupancy rates, this one asserts the need without measuring it. That is not a reason to doubt the need — Talayan appears in the parliamentary districts schedule with 34,156 people and the province's hospital provision is documented as thin throughout this registry — but a committee choosing among a dozen competing hospital bills has nothing here to weigh.

The emergencies and disasters clause is the provision to keep, and its history in this registry is instructive. The same sentence appears in the bill that became BAA 69, where it survived into the enacted act. A hospital whose statutory purpose expressly includes disaster response has a basis for stockpiling, for surge planning and for claiming calamity funds that a hospital established only for ordinary care does not — and in the Maguindanao lowlands, where flooding displaces communities most years, that is a practical difference rather than a rhetorical one.

The appropriation language matters for the same reason it does in the companion bills filed that season: funding "its facilities and professional health care, medical personnel" rather than the hospital in the abstract. Several members converged on that formulation in early 2023, which suggests a shared diagnosis that the region's problem was never the designation but the staffing that failed to follow it.

Communities affected by flooding and displacement, addressed through the emergencies and disasters clause.

readings.insight:
The name is worth noting plainly, because the registry rewards attention to it. The municipality is Datu Anggal Midtimbang and the bill's author is MP Tawakal B. Midtimbang. A member filing to build a hospital in the municipality that carries their family name is unremarkable in Philippine local politics and worth recording in a reading whose purpose is to show what the documents say — particularly since the measure appropriates for a facility twice the size the municipality's population supports.

Against that, the need is real on the registry's own evidence. Datu Anggal Midtimbang sits in the first district of Maguindanao del Sur, alongside South Upi, Talayan, Guindulungan, Datu Unsay and Datu Hoffer Ampatuan — a district of roughly 170,000 people in which this registry records no hospital act at all, while the neighbouring northern district of Maguindanao del Norte has 2 hospitals and 4 further bills seeking more. The question a committee would have to answer is not whether the municipality needs a facility but whether 50 beds there is a better use of the money than 25 beds there and 25 somewhere else.

All 3 municipalities are small. The Parliamentary Districts Act prints Talayan at 34,156, Guindulungan at 24,933 and Datu Anggal Midtimbang at 28,224. On the Department of Health ratio of 1 bed per 1,000 that other bills in this registry invoke, each supports about 25 to 34 beds — so a 50-bed request is roughly double what the municipality's own population implies, and the bills do not explain the margin.

MP Midtimbang filed 3 hospital bills on the same template. Bill No. 156 establishes a 50-bed Level I hospital at Talayan, Bill No. 157 at Datu Anggal Midtimbang and Bill No. 158 at Guindulungan — all in the Maguindanao provinces, all 50 beds, all with the same declaration of policy and the same Universal Health Care integration clause. The Talayan bill reached Second Reading; these 2 are still at First Reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
This institutionalises a community dispute-resolution system called PASAD — the People’s Alternative System in Addressing Disputes — and builds an office to run it in every province and municipality of the region.

The purpose section states the aim plainly: that people take genuine steps to resolve disputes before certain court actions are begun, and that parties keep the autonomy to settle their differences by a process they agree on. Parties may agree that a dispute is resolved by PASAD; the Ministry of Public Order and Safety then facilitates the constitution of the PASAD Provider the parties choose, and appoints one itself if the parties cannot agree. Providers must be neutral, preferably accredited by MPOS, at least 30 years old, and unrelated by blood or marriage to either party within the third degree.

The process is bounded by confidentiality, with stated exceptions and a waiver mechanism, and by a right of recusal. Where it succeeds, the parties sign a written settlement agreement, the Provider authenticates it and gives them copies, and they may deposit it with the appropriate office where one of them resides. If it has to be enforced, a party may petition a court and may ask the Ministry for help enforcing it.

Section 19 is the section that makes this a Bangsamoro law rather than a generic mediation statute. The Ministry must ensure the PASAD procedure on conciliation, peacemaking and amicable settlement accords with Islamic law — sulh, the tradition of reconciliation — and must also promote the traditional methods used by non-Moro indigenous peoples.

The structure is a Regional Office for PASAD under MPOS, with a secretariat under an Executive Director and three departments: Finance and Administration; Training, Accreditation and Promotion; and Policy, Compliance and Monitoring. Below it sits a Provincial Office under a Provincial Administrator in every BARMM province including the Special Geographic Area, and a Municipal Coordinating Office in every cluster or municipality.
readings.whyProposed:
The stated purpose is speedy, impartial and inexpensive justice through early dispute resolution, and — in the bill’s own phrase — justpeace and sustainable development in the region.

The unstated context is what makes it serious. Formal courts are distant, slow and expensive for most of this region, and disputes that go unresolved here do not simply persist: they escalate into rido, the clan feuding that is among the largest causes of violence and displacement in the Bangsamoro. Sulh and traditional settlement are how most disputes have always actually been resolved. The bill is an attempt to give that a statutory footing, a trained and accredited cadre, and an office structure reaching down to the municipality.
whoIsAffected: Parties to disputes across the region, who gain a settlement route that is faster and cheaper than a court.
Communities affected by rido, where an unsettled dispute is the first step in a feud.
Non-Moro indigenous peoples, whose traditional dispute processes the Ministry is required to promote.
PASAD Providers, a new accredited role with stated qualifications and a recusal duty.

The Ministry of Public Order and Safety, which would carry a regional office, a provincial office in every province and the Special Geographic Area, and a municipal coordinating office in every municipality or cluster.
The courts, which the system is designed to keep certain disputes out of.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Order and Safety (MPOS), which accredits and where necessary appoints Providers
Regional Office for PASAD under MPOS, with an Executive Director and three service departments
PASAD Provincial Offices under Provincial Administrators, in every province and in the Special Geographic Area
Municipal Coordinating Offices for PASAD in every municipality or cluster
A Technical Working Group organized by the Chief Minister within 1 month of approval, to draft the implementing rules, with an Oversight Committee

funding.detail: No figure. The amount necessary is to be included in the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act of the year following enactment and thereafter — which means, unusually, the Act carries no first-year money at all and the whole structure waits for the next budget cycle. For a bill that creates a regional office, a provincial office in every province and a coordinating office in every municipality, that is a substantial standing cost with no stated size and a one-year delay built into the text.

whatChanges: PASAD becomes a recognized route to settling a dispute, agreed to by the parties.
A settlement reached through it is a written, authenticated agreement that a court can be asked to enforce.
The procedure must be aligned with Islamic law on conciliation and peacemaking, and traditional non-Moro indigenous methods must be promoted.
Providers become an accredited role with stated qualifications, a recusal right and a confidentiality duty.
MPOS gains a PASAD office structure reaching from the region to the municipality.
The Office may recommend statutory changes on dispute resolution directly to Parliament.
readings.insight:
The most consequential thing in this bill is Section 19, and it is one paragraph long. It requires that the whole procedure accord with Islamic law on conciliation and peacemaking, and separately that traditional methods among non-Moro indigenous peoples be promoted. That is the difference between a mediation statute and a Bangsamoro one — it takes sulh, which is how disputes here have in practice always been settled, and gives it a place inside the formal system rather than beside it.

What the bill does not do is make PASAD compulsory. The purpose section says people should take genuine steps to resolve disputes "before certain court actions are instituted", but the operative provision begins with the parties agreeing. No category of dispute is required to go through PASAD first, and no court is directed to send anything to it. Compared with the barangay justice system under national law, which does bar certain suits until conciliation has been attempted, this is an invitation rather than a gate — and the gap between the aspiration in Section 2 and the mechanism in Section 8 is where the bill will be tested.

The funding clause is the practical worry. An office in every province and every municipality is a real payroll, and the Act deliberately takes no money in its first year, deferring everything to the following budget. A dispute-resolution system that exists in law and not yet in the municipalities is worse than none, because parties will have been told to use something that has no one to staff it.

On its progress: filed March 2023, First Reading May 2023, and referred to the Committees on the Bangsamoro Justice System and on Finance in October 2024, where the index leaves it.

readings.whatItDoes:
This proposes to integrate zakat — the obligatory almsgiving of Islam — with the individual income tax paid by Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government.

The mechanism is set out plainly. An employee’s income tax is reduced by an amount equal to the zakat they pay. The finance officer of the office deducts both, remits the income tax to the Bureau of Internal Revenue, and remits the zakat to the Office of the Lujnatul Uliya of the place, or to its authorised collector. Zakat is computed at 2.5% of net — not gross — income, following the majority Sunni position, which the bill states.

Coverage is confined to government service under BARMM: regular and semi-regular employees, permanent or contractual, and holders of political and appointive positions.

The bill knows it has a problem, and says so. Section 9 requires a representative of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government to sit together and settle the issues. Section 10 then provides that, pending that settlement and national approval, ₱25,000,000 shall be appropriated annually as a subsidy to cover the income tax not remitted to the BIR — the region paying the Bureau the difference, so that no national revenue is lost while the question is unresolved.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section frames it as moral governance: merging what it treats as two obligations of the same character — both, in the bill’s reasoning, levies for public use and public purpose — into a single obligation, so a Muslim employee is not paying twice. The justification section calls the present arrangement a duplicity of obligation and argues that removing it is consistent with the Philippine law of taxation being progressive, regressive and uniform.

Underneath is a real situation. Observant Muslim employees in the region pay income tax to the state and zakat to their community, and for many the combined burden is the reason zakat goes unpaid or is paid without record.
whoIsAffected: Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government — regular, semi-regular, permanent, contractual, political and appointive.
The Office of the Lujnatul Uliya and its authorised zakat collectors, who would receive remitted zakat through a government payroll.
Finance officers in every Bangsamoro government office, who would deduct and remit both.
The Bureau of Internal Revenue, whose collection from these employees would be made whole by a regional subsidy rather than by the taxpayer.
Non-Muslim employees of the Bangsamoro Government, who are outside the scheme.
The national government, whose agreement Section 9 requires.
implementedBy: Finance officers of Bangsamoro government offices, who deduct and remit
Office of the Lujnatul Uliya, and its authorised collectors of zakat
Bureau of Internal Revenue, which continues to receive the tax — via the subsidy, pending settlement
A joint discussion of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government, required by Section 9

funding.detail: ₱25,000,000 annually, appropriated as a subsidy to pay the Bureau of Internal Revenue the income tax that employees do not remit because they have paid zakat instead. The subsidy is expressly a holding arrangement — it runs "pending settlement of the issues and approval thereof by the National Government". It is one of the few precise figures in this batch and it buys time rather than a service.

whatChanges: A Muslim employee’s income tax is reduced by the zakat they pay, at 2.5% of net income.
Zakat is deducted at payroll and remitted to the Lujnatul Uliya by the employing office.
The Bangsamoro Government appropriates ₱25 million a year to make the BIR whole in the meantime.
The Bangsamoro Parliament, the Darul Ifta and the national government are required to meet and settle the legal question.
readings.insight:
This is the most legally exposed bill in this batch, and the striking thing is that its drafters clearly knew it.

Individual income tax is a national tax, imposed by the National Internal Revenue Code and collected by the BIR. A regional parliament cannot reduce a national tax liability, and the Bangsamoro Organic Law does not give the region that power. The bill does not pretend otherwise. Section 9 requires the region, the Darul Ifta and the national government to sit down over it, and Section 10 provides ₱25 million a year so that until they do, the national treasury loses nothing and the employee’s zakat still reaches the Lujnatul Uliya. That is an unusually honest structure: it converts a jurisdictional claim the region cannot yet make into a subsidy the region can pay, and it leaves the constitutional question open on the face of the statute.

The second question is one the bill does not address. The scheme routes a payroll deduction from a government office to a religious body, and confers a fiscal benefit that depends on the employee’s religion. Those raise establishment and equal protection questions under the Constitution that Section 9’s discussion would have to reach.

A drafting point that matters practically: the bill repeatedly says "individual income tax return" where it means the tax itself. A return is a form. The distinction would need fixing before enactment, because the operative sections deduct and remit something that, as written, is a document.

On its progress: filed February 2023, First Reading May 2023, deferred in July 2025.

readings.whatItDoes:
This increases the bed capacity of the Luuk District Hospital at Tubig Putih in Luuk, Sulu, with the facilities and professional complement raised commensurately and future growth tied to the hospital development plan.

The bill is the most quantitatively argued hospital measure in the registry. It works from Department of Health Administrative Order 2006-0004, the guidelines for issuing a certificate of need to establish a new hospital, which set the ratio at no more than 1 bed per 1,000 population.

Against that standard: Sulu has 1,000,108 people and 320 beds — a deficit of 680. Counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the establishment of the Maimbung District Hospital still leaves 480 missing. And the eastern part of the island is served by a 25-bed infirmary and a 25-bed Level I district hospital for 4 municipalities — Luuk, Old Panamao, Kalingalan Caluang and the coastal municipality of Omar — holding more than 155,000 people across over 900 square kilometers.
readings.whyProposed:
The note makes its case through a single event. A patient must travel more than an hour to reach the Provincial Hospital in Jolo when the Luuk District Hospital is overwhelmed and cannot transfer them to the Panamao infirmary — "just like what happened during the onslaught of the COVID-19 Pandemic". In emergent situations, the note says, that travel time can mean life and death.

The argument for upgrading rather than building is practical. As a Level I district hospital, Luuk already provides major and minor surgery, emergency care, obstetric and neonatal care, laboratory testing, outpatient and even dental services. The capability exists; the beds, staff and equipment do not.
whoIsAffected: The 155,000 people of Luuk, Old Panamao, Kalingalan Caluang and Omar, across more than 900 square kilometers.
Patients travelling over an hour to Jolo when the district hospital is full.
The 25-bed infirmary at Panamao, which cannot absorb overflow.
The Sulu Provincial Hospital in Jolo, which receives what eastern Sulu cannot handle.
The Ministry of Health, which would fund the additional beds, staff and equipment.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the figure is left to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: Eastern Sulu's district hospital gains beds, staff and equipment.
A facility already capable of surgery and obstetrics gets the capacity to use those services.
Growth is tied to a hospital development plan rather than to further legislation.
readings.insight:
Upgrading a hospital that already has the clinical capability is the most efficient hospital proposal in this registry, and the bill makes the argument explicitly. Luuk can already perform major and minor surgery, deliver babies, run a laboratory and see outpatients — it simply cannot admit enough people. Adding beds to an existing Level I facility buys clinical capacity that building a new 25-bed hospital elsewhere would not, because the new hospital would need the theatre, the laboratory and the staff from scratch.

The COVID example is the most concrete failure documented in any of these bills. The note does not argue hypothetically about overcrowding; it records that the district hospital was overwhelmed, that the Panamao infirmary could not take the transfers, and that the alternative was more than an hour to Jolo. That is a referral chain breaking under load, witnessed, and it is the strongest evidence a hospital bill in this registry offers.

Sulu's arithmetic is set out in Bill No. 161 and it frames all 4 of the province's hospital bills in this registry. The province has 1,000,108 people and 320 hospital beds. On the Department of Health's own standard — Administrative Order 2006-0004, 1 bed per 1,000 population — that is a shortfall of 680 beds, and even counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the new Maimbung District Hospital, 480 are still missing.

What the bill does not say is how many beds it asks for. It increases capacity, raises facilities and staffing commensurately, and ties future growth to the development plan — without naming a number. Against the Ambolodto bills, which compute a deficit and state the beds sought, that is a gap: a measure this well argued on the arithmetic leaves its own ask unquantified.

readings.whatItDoes:
This upgrades the Parang District Hospital in Parang, Sulu, increasing its authorised bed capacity for general care services to 50 — from the 10 it currently holds.

A district hospital authorised for 10 beds is, in practice, an infirmary with a district hospital's name, and the bill's purpose is to bring the authorisation up to the number a Level I facility serving a municipality needs.
readings.whyProposed:
Parang is a municipality of Sulu — not to be confused with the Parang in Maguindanao del Norte where the region's seat of government is to be established — and its district hospital carries an authorised capacity of 10 beds.

The case is the same arithmetic its companion bill sets out for the province as a whole: Sulu has about 320 beds for over a million people, and a district hospital authorised for 10 of them contributes almost nothing to closing that gap.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Parang, Sulu, served by a district hospital authorised for 10 beds.
Patients referred to Jolo because the district hospital cannot admit them.
The Sulu Provincial Hospital, which absorbs what the district hospitals cannot.
The Ministry of Health, which would fund a fivefold increase in capacity.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the figure is left to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: A district hospital's authorised capacity rises from 10 beds to 50.
General care services gain the capacity to admit patients rather than refer them.
readings.insight:
Ten beds is the number to hold onto, because it shows what "district hospital" can mean in this region. A district hospital is meant to be the referral facility for a cluster of municipalities; authorised at 10 beds it cannot be the referral facility for one. The same member filed Bill No. 161 for the Luuk District Hospital in the same province on the same subject, and together the 2 describe a provincial hospital system in which the district tier barely exists.

Sulu's arithmetic is set out in Bill No. 161 and it frames all 4 of the province's hospital bills in this registry. The province has 1,000,108 people and 320 hospital beds. On the Department of Health's own standard — Administrative Order 2006-0004, 1 bed per 1,000 population — that is a shortfall of 680 beds, and even counting the 200 beds expected from the Sulu Provincial Hospital upgrade and the new Maimbung District Hospital, 480 are still missing.

The jump from 10 to 50 is the largest proportional increase sought by any hospital bill in this registry — fivefold — and it is also the one most likely to be reduced. The pattern in the enacted acts is convergence on 25 beds to national minimum standards: the South Ubian and Sibutu bills each asked 50 and received 25, while the Pura bill asked 10 to 15 and received 25. On that record a 10-bed hospital asking for 50 would most likely come out at 25, which would still be a substantial gain.

One point of care for anyone searching the registry: there are 2 Parangs. This bill concerns Parang in Sulu. The Parang in Maguindanao del Norte is where BAA 37 establishes the region's seat of government, where the Iranon District Hospital was converted to a 200-bed provincial hospital by BAA 73, and where Bongo Island lies — the subject of Bill No. 269. Four separate measures in this registry turn on the 2 names.
