readings.whatItDoes:
This establishes a district hospital in Languyan, Tawi-Tawi, to be known as the Languyan District Hospital — a Level 1 facility of 50 beds.

What distinguishes the drafting is that it works from the standard rather than asserting a level. The note sets out what the Department of Health requires a Level 1 district hospital to have by way of clinical services, and the bill is written to that specification.
readings.whyProposed:
Languyan covers 581.20 square kilometers — 224.40 square miles — which is 16.03% of the province's land area, with a population of 37,096 at the 2020 census.

The case is the familiar island-province one: a municipality holding a sixth of Tawi-Tawi's territory and more than 37,000 people, whose patients must reach the provincial hospital at Bongo for anything a health unit cannot handle. The bill is presented as the answer to that gap, sized and specified to the national standard for the level it claims.
whoIsAffected: The 37,096 residents of Languyan, across 16.03% of Tawi-Tawi's land area.
Patients currently travelling to the provincial hospital in Bongao.
The Datu Halun Sakilan Memorial Hospital, already documented elsewhere in this registry as running at 150 to 200% occupancy.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the hospital and staff it to Level 1 clinical standards.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the facility and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Languyan gains a 50-bed Level 1 district hospital.
The facility is specified against the Department of Health's own clinical service requirements for the level.
Pressure eases on the overloaded provincial hospital at Bongao.
readings.insight:
Setting out the Department of Health's clinical service requirements in the note is the practice that ought to be standard and almost never is. A bill that says "Level 1 district hospital" is asking for a label; a bill that lists the clinical services the label requires is asking for a facility, and it gives the health ministry and the finance ministry something to cost. Of the 23 hospital bills in this registry, this is 1 of only 2 that engage with what a level actually means — the other being the Maguindanao Provincial Hospital upgrade, which reproduces the administrative order.

The land-area figure is the argument that a population count alone would miss. Languyan is 16% of Tawi-Tawi spread across a province of islands, so the distance a patient travels is not from Languyan to Bongao but from wherever in Languyan they live to the sea, and then across it. A single district hospital in the municipality does not solve that for the furthest barangays, and no bill in this registry addresses intra-municipal distance in an island setting.

The co-authorship is worth a note: 5 principal authors and 13 co-authors, including most of the members who filed the island hospital bills separately. A measure with that much of the chamber's name on it and 3 years at Committee Stage says something about the difference between signing a bill and moving it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 163, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the Bangsamoro Fast Food Labeling Act, and it does something none of the other food bills does: it names the companies.

Section 3 applies the Act to fast food restaurants "including but not limited to Jollibee, McDonalds, Chowking, Greenwich Pizza, Mang Inasal, KFC, Goldilocks, Red Ribbon, Pizza Hut, and Shakeys", whether inside or outside malls, operating anywhere in the region. A fast food restaurant is then defined by 6 characteristics — quick service, food already prepared or quickly preparable, disposable wrappings and utensils, preparation encouraging consumption off the premises, orders not taken at the table, and an asset size of ₱5,000,000 or above.

The labelling rule has 2 halves and the first is the important one. Food items and condiments are *presumed not to contain* pork, lard or any by-product unless labelled otherwise, and the bill states the consequence expressly: "The lack of label is equivalent to a claim on the absence of the aforementioned ingredients." Anything that does contain pork must be labelled "WITH PORK" or words to that effect — on advertisements and on promotional and marketing materials distributed anywhere in the region, in the menus in every branch, and in the eMenus of online food platforms, with GrabFood and foodpanda named. Management is responsible for ensuring the label is printed or shown conspicuously enough to be read and understood by an ordinary person.

Prohibited acts are failing to label a pork-containing item in advertisements, materials, menus or eMenus; falsely claiming a food item or condiment contains no pork; and violating the implementing rules. Penalties escalate: ₱10,000 to ₱20,000 for a first offence, ₱20,000 to ₱50,000 for a second, ₱50,000 to ₱100,000 for a third, imposed on the owner or, for a corporate entity, on the directors, officers, employees or persons responsible. On a third or later offence the Council may recommend suspension of operations for up to 6 months, or cancellation of licences or permits, to the local government concerned.

A Fast Food Labeling Council enforces it, chaired by the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism with the Minister of Health as vice-chair and the interior ministry among its members.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy is consumer education and protection, and the mechanism chosen is disclosure rather than prohibition: the Act regulates the labelling, display and advertisement of food products and condiments by popular fast food chains in the region.

The practical problem is specific. National fast food chains operate standard menus across the Philippines, and a Muslim customer in Cotabato City ordering from the same board as a customer in Manila has no way of knowing which items contain pork or lard. The bill does not ask the chains to change what they sell; it asks them to say what is in it, in every place a customer might look — including the delivery apps.
whoIsAffected: Muslim consumers in the region ordering from national fast food chains.
The 10 named chains and any other quick-service restaurant with assets of ₱5,000,000 or more.
Owners and, for corporate operators, directors, officers and responsible employees, who bear the penalties personally.
Online food platforms including GrabFood and foodpanda, whose eMenus must carry the labels.
Advertisers and marketers distributing promotional material in the region.
Small eateries below the ₱5,000,000 asset threshold, which fall outside the Act.
implementedBy: Fast Food Labeling Council, chaired by the Minister of Trade, Investments and Tourism with the Minister of Health as Vice Chairperson and the interior ministry among its members
Local government units, to which the Council may recommend suspension of operations or cancellation of permits
Fast food management, expressly made responsible for the conspicuousness of the labelling

funding.detail: No appropriation. The scheme is funded by nothing and enforced by escalating fines — ₱10,000 to ₱20,000, then ₱20,000 to ₱50,000, then ₱50,000 to ₱100,000 — with suspension of operations for up to 6 months or cancellation of permits available on a third or later offence.

whatChanges: Pork-containing items must be labelled "WITH PORK" in menus, eMenus, advertisements and marketing materials in the region.
An unlabelled item legally represents itself as pork-free.
Delivery platform listings come within the labelling duty.
Named national chains are brought under a regional labelling regime enforced by a ministerial council.
Repeat offenders risk suspension or loss of their business permits.
readings.insight:
The default presumption is the legally interesting move and it is easy to read past. Most labelling statutes require a disclosure and punish its absence. This one goes further: it declares that the absence of a label is itself a positive claim that the food contains no pork. That converts every unlabelled item on every menu into a representation the chain has made, which means a mislabelled item is not merely an omission but a false claim — and it is what allows the second prohibited act, falsely claiming an item contains no pork, to bite without anyone having to prove the chain said anything at all.

Naming the 10 companies in the statute is unusual and cuts 2 ways. It removes any argument about coverage — Jollibee cannot contend it is not a fast food restaurant within the meaning of the Act — and it dates the law to the brands trading in 2023, while the "including but not limited to" and the 6-characteristic definition are what carry it forward. The ₱5,000,000 asset threshold is the real line, and it deliberately exempts the small local eatery, which is the sensible half of the design: a family carinderia cannot maintain compliant eMenu labelling across delivery platforms.

Extending the duty to eMenus and naming GrabFood and foodpanda is the provision that makes this bill current rather than a decade behind the market. A consumer ordering through an app never sees the in-store menu board, and a labelling law confined to premises would have missed the fastest-growing way food is sold. Few statutes in this registry engage with the platform economy at all.

What the bill does not do is address halal more broadly, and that is a deliberate narrowing. Pork is the clearest case and the easiest to label; the harder questions — slaughter method, cross-contamination, gelatine and other derivatives — are exactly what Bill No. 10's certification scheme and Bill No. 60's prohibited acts are built for. Read together the 3 bills are close to a complete scheme, and taken one at a time each has an obvious gap.

Three bills in this registry regulate what the region eats, and they pick 3 different instruments for the same problem. Bill No. 10 licenses: every Muslim restaurant must hold an annual halal certificate. Bill No. 60 polices the lie: no certificate is required, but misrepresenting food as halal becomes an offence with a long schedule of prohibited acts. Bill No. 164 discloses: it does not regulate halal at all, instead requiring named fast food chains to label anything containing pork. All 3 are at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and none of the 3 has become law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 164, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This gives Bangsamoro voters the power to make regional law themselves, and sets out every step of how.

The power covers propositions to enact, amend or repeal regional legislation, and is exercised by registered voters of the region. Five things are off limits, among them propositions embracing more than one subject and propositions outside the powers of the Bangsamoro Government or inside the reserved powers of the national government.

The procedure runs like this. Proponents first send the proposed text to the Bangsamoro Attorney General and ask for a circulating title and summary and a unique numerical identifier. Once issued, they have 180 days to gather signatures. The petition is filed with the Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which certifies whether it is sufficient and whether the signatures are authentic. An Initiatives Coordinator is provided for.

The threshold is the heart of it: a proposition qualifies as a ballot measure if signed by at least 10% of all registered voters of the region, reckoned from the immediately preceding election, and — for propositions affecting the whole region — every parliamentary district must be represented by at least 3%. A plebiscite follows.

The bill then does something a plain initiative statute would not. Section 18 limits Parliament: a proposition approved by initiative cannot be repealed, modified or amended within 6 months, may only be repealed by Parliament within 3 years, and any law seeking to repeal a law enacted by initiative is itself subject to a referendum. Section 19 provides a separate, gentler route — a people-initiated bill, filed by petition with Parliament for it to consider in the ordinary way.
readings.whyProposed: The Bangsamoro Organic Law contemplates a system of initiative and referendum for the region, and until it is legislated the power exists on paper and cannot be exercised. This bill supplies the machinery: who may propose, what may be proposed, how a petition is titled and circulated, how many signatures are needed and from where, who certifies them, and what happens after a proposition passes.
whoIsAffected: Every registered voter in the Bangsamoro, who gains a route to legislate directly.
The Bangsamoro Parliament, whose power to amend or repeal a successful initiative is expressly restricted for 3 years.
The Bangsamoro Attorney General, given the gatekeeping function of issuing the circulating title and summary.
The Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which must verify signatures at region-wide scale and run the plebiscites.
Civil society and advocacy groups, for whom this is the mechanism to put a measure Parliament will not take up to a vote.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Electoral Office, which certifies sufficiency and authenticity and conducts the plebiscite
Office of the Bangsamoro Attorney General, which issues the circulating title, the summary and the numerical identifier
An Initiatives Coordinator provided for in the Act
The Bangsamoro Parliament, for the people-initiated bill route and for the adoption provision

funding.detail: No figure. Initial implementation is charged against the current year’s appropriations of the agencies named in the Act, and later years go into the Bangsamoro General Appropriations Act. Verifying signatures from 10% of the region’s registered voters and running a region-wide plebiscite are both expensive, and the cost falls first on the Bangsamoro Electoral Office out of a budget already set.

whatChanges: Registered voters can propose regional legislation directly and put it to a plebiscite.
A proposition needs 10% of the region’s registered voters, with at least 3% from every parliamentary district for region-wide measures.
Proponents get 180 days to gather signatures after the Attorney General issues the circulating title.
Parliament cannot touch a successful initiative for 6 months and can only repeal it within 3 years — and a repealing law must itself go to a referendum.
A separate route lets voters file a bill with Parliament by petition.
Propositions embracing more than one subject, or outside Bangsamoro competence, are barred.
readings.insight:
The district floor is the design decision that will decide whether this power is ever used. Requiring 10% of all registered voters region-wide is a high bar on its own; requiring in addition that every parliamentary district supply at least 3% means an initiative cannot be carried by a concentrated majority in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao alone. It has to reach into the island districts and into every constituency. That is a deliberate protection for the smaller and more distant parts of the region against a mainland majority, and it is also, in a region with this geography and these transport costs, a very hard signature drive to run.

Section 18 is the more unusual provision and it is genuinely strong. Most initiative statutes let the legislature amend what the people pass; this one bars Parliament from touching it for 6 months, restricts repeal to a 3-year window, and then requires any repealing law to go to a referendum of its own. That makes a successful initiative harder to undo than an ordinary act of Parliament, which is a real transfer of power away from the chamber that would be passing this bill.

Worth noting what it does not cover. Section 4 confines the power to regional legislation and leaves initiatives on all other legislative acts to existing law, so this is not a route to amending the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which is national legislation.

On its progress: filed March 2023, First Reading June 2023, deferred in August 2024 and referred to the Committee on Rules that same month, where it sits.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 165, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is MP Froilyn Mendoza's indigenous peoples code — 14 chapters recognising the rights of non-Moro indigenous peoples and creating a Ministry for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples Affairs to administer them.

The ministry is the structural choice the whole bill turns on. Section 51 creates the MNMIPA as the primary government agency responsible for policies, plans and programmes for non-Moro indigenous peoples specifically — a ministry of their own, not a bureau inside a larger one.

The chapters run from ancestral domains and the indigenous concept of ownership, through self-governance and empowerment, the traditional or tribal justice system, social justice and human rights, cultural integrity and identity, the ministry itself, delineation and recognition of domains, enforcement, the Ancestral Domains Fund, penalties, intergovernmental relations and final provisions.

Two figures carry most of the bill's weight. Section 11 gives non-Moro indigenous peoples and communities an equitable share of revenue from the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources within their titled territories of "no less than fifty percent (50%)", determined by the new ministry. And Section 78 creates an Ancestral Domain Fund with an initial ₱200,000,000 for compensation for expropriated lands, delineation and development — expressly to be taken from the Bangsamoro Government's Block Grant.

The penalties run from 9 months to 15 years' imprisonment, or a fine of ₱500,000 to ₱1,000,000, or both, with customary law applied first subject to bars on cruel or degrading punishment, the death penalty and excessive fines. Officers of a juridical offender are personally liable and their certificates and licences cancellable.

Chapter XIII builds a channel the bill calls intergovernmental relations: a Council or Consultative Body for each non-Moro tribe, members selected under their own customary laws, advising the Minister — and expressly able to lobby the Chief Minister where a policy violates their rights, with the ministry funding the convening.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration reaffirms the 1987 Constitution, the national Indigenous Peoples Rights Act, Muslim Mindanao Act 241 — the ARMM-era Tribal Peoples Rights Act — the Organic Law, and international instruments including International Labour Organization Convention No. 169 and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Its operative claim is about identity rather than services: non-Moro indigenous peoples are to have the freedom to retain their distinct indigenous and ethnic identity *in addition to* their Bangsamoro political identity, with no discrimination on the basis of identity, religion or ethnicity.

That sentence is the bill. The Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo, Erumanun ne Menuvu, Higaonon and B'laan are not Muslim and were not party to the conflict the region was created to settle, and the fear the bill addresses is that a Bangsamoro government will serve them as a minority within a Moro framework rather than as peoples with their own standing.
whoIsAffected: The non-Moro indigenous peoples of the region — Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo, Erumanun ne Menuvu, Higaonon and B'laan.
Companies extracting natural resources in ancestral domains, who would owe no less than half the revenue.
Each non-Moro tribe, which gains a council selected under its own customary law with a channel to the Chief Minister.
The existing Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs, whose non-Moro mandate would move to a new ministry.
Marginalized Moro communities — Sama Dilaut, Jama Mapun and others — who are outside this bill's coverage.
The Bangsamoro Block Grant, from which the ₱200 million domain fund would be taken.
implementedBy: Ministry for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples Affairs (MNMIPA), created by the Act as the primary agency for non-Moro indigenous peoples
Councils or Consultative Bodies for each non-Moro tribe, selected under customary law, advising the Minister and able to lobby the Chief Minister
Traditional or tribal justice systems, applying customary law in the first instance
An Ancestral Domain Fund of ₱200 million drawn from the Block Grant

funding.detail: An Ancestral Domain Fund with an initial ₱200,000,000 for compensation for expropriated lands, delineation and development of domains, expressly charged to the Bangsamoro Government's Block Grant. Separately, communities are to receive no less than 50% of revenue from natural resources extracted in their titled territories, determined by the new ministry — a transfer rather than an appropriation, and much the larger sum.

whatChanges: Non-Moro indigenous peoples gain a ministry of their own rather than a share of an existing one.
Communities receive at least half the revenue from resources taken from their domains.
Each tribe gains a council chosen under its own customary law, funded to meet and able to lobby the Chief Minister.
Penalties for intrusion on ancestral domains reach 15 years and ₱1 million.
ILO Convention 169 enters the region's policy framework alongside UNDRIP.
readings.insight:
Fifty percent against ten percent is the difference that matters most, and it is the clearest measurable gap between any 2 competing bills in this registry. This bill gives communities no less than half the revenue from resources extracted in their ancestral domains. The cabinet's Bill No. 273, filed 9 months later, set the floor at 10% — and that is the version Parliament enacted as BAA 64 in December 2024. On the single question of what an indigenous community is owed for what is taken from its land, the enacted law delivers a fifth of what the indigenous members' own bill proposed.

The ministry is the deeper disagreement. This bill creates a Ministry for Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples Affairs, on the premise that non-Moro peoples need an institution answerable to them alone. BAA 64 took the opposite path: it strengthens the single Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and widens its coverage to include Badjao, Sama Dilaut, Jama Mapun, Sama Banguingui and Sama Pangutaran alongside the non-Moro groups, declaring the whole territory the shared ancestral domain of all peoples with pre-colonial ties. That is a defensible and generous architecture, and it is also precisely the subsuming this bill was written to prevent.

Which reading is right is a political question this registry cannot settle. What it can record is who proposed what. MP Mendoza holds 1 of the 2 parliamentary seats reserved for non-Moro indigenous peoples under the Organic Law, and she filed this in April 2023. The Government of the Day filed its own version in January 2024 and had it enacted inside 11 months. The reserved-seat mechanism gave non-Moro peoples a voice that produced a complete legislative text, and the text that became law was the cabinet's.

Chapter XIII deserves attention as the provision most likely to have survived scrutiny on its merits. Councils constituted per tribe under each tribe's own customary law, funded by the ministry to convene, advising the Minister and expressly entitled to lobby the Chief Minister when a policy violates their rights, is a more robust consultation design than a seat on a board — it keeps the selection inside the community and routes the grievance above the ministry that might be the problem. Nothing equivalent appears in the enacted act.

One point of continuity worth noting: this bill cites Muslim Mindanao Act 241, the ARMM's Tribal Peoples Rights Act, which BAA 64 repealed and replaced. Both measures understood themselves as succeeding that statute. They disagreed about what should succeed it.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 64, the enacted indigenous peoples act

readings.whatItDoes:
The Madaris Education Assistance Act of 2023 puts money into private Islamic schools — madaris — by paying three different recipients directly.

Students get tuition of not less than ₱1,000 a year, reading materials, and a nutrition and feeding program for the young ones. Teachers — gurus, the bill uses the Arabic term and defines it — get an allowance of not less than ₱2,000 a month plus a faculty education development program. The madrasah itself gets classroom facilities, named down to desks, tables and chalkboards, and textbook assistance.

The faculty program is the most substantial piece: scholarships for master’s and doctorate degrees, in the country and outside it, plus seminars and training. Anyone who qualifies to study abroad must sign an undertaking to return and serve for a period set against the length of the scholarship.

Eligibility is narrow and stated. Priority goes to students whose family income is not more than ₱40,000 a year. Assistance runs only to Muslim students who are Filipino citizens and residents of the Bangsamoro, who are not already receiving another government scholarship, who are enrolled in a madrasah, and who have not transferred to one outside the region. MBHTE, through the Bureau of Madaris Education, sets the criteria, accredits which madaris qualify, and assesses whether the schools receiving the money are still teaching well.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section grounds it in Section 16, Article IX of the Bangsamoro Organic Law — the mandate to establish and maintain a complete and adequate system of education responsive to the needs and aspirations of the Bangsamoro people — and says the way to improve quality in the madaris is to assist the teachers and the students directly.

The unstated premise is that madaris are community-based and privately operated. They sit outside the public school funding system, they teach a large share of Bangsamoro children, and until something like this passes there is no standing mechanism for regional money to reach them.
whoIsAffected: Students in madaris across the region, with priority to those whose family income is ₱40,000 a year or less.
Gurus, who would receive a monthly allowance and access to postgraduate scholarships abroad.
Madaris as institutions, which would receive classroom furniture and textbooks.
Students already holding another government scholarship, who are expressly excluded.
Non-Muslim students, who are outside the stated coverage.
MBHTE and the Bureau of Madaris Education, which would have to build an accreditation system to run any of it.
implementedBy: Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education (MBHTE), for policy guidance, monitoring and the implementing rules
Bureau of Madaris Education (BME), which delivers the assistance and, with MBHTE, sets the income criterion

funding.detail: No total is stated. MBHTE determines the amount necessary for initial implementation, and later years go into the annual Bangsamoro appropriations. The only hard figures in the bill are the floors on individual benefits — not less than ₱1,000 per student per year and not less than ₱2,000 per guru per month — and the ₱40,000 annual family income mark that sets priority.

whatChanges: Regional money reaches privately operated madaris for the first time through a standing mechanism.
Gurus gain a monthly allowance with a floor of ₱2,000 and access to postgraduate scholarships.
Students in madaris gain a tuition subsidy, reading materials and a feeding program.
MBHTE must build an accreditation policy to determine which madaris qualify.
Assistance is conditioned on continued quality, which MBHTE is required to assess.
readings.insight:
Every benefit in this bill is a floor rather than a figure. Not less than ₱1,000 a year, not less than ₱2,000 a month: generous drafting in one sense, because nothing caps what MBHTE may pay, and empty in another, because the bill sets no total and MBHTE decides the initial appropriation itself. What the law guarantees is a minimum per head; what it costs is settled somewhere else entirely.

The floors themselves are worth reading against the region. ₱1,000 a year in tuition and ₱2,000 a month for a teacher are modest sums, and the ₱40,000 annual family income that triggers priority is well under the national poverty threshold for a family of five — which means the priority mark will catch a very large share of the households the bill is aimed at rather than distinguishing between them.

The scholarship clause is the quiet ambition in it. Master’s and doctorate study abroad for madrasah teachers, with a return-service undertaking, is a serious investment in a teaching corps that has largely had no route to formal postgraduate credentials.

The coverage clause runs to Muslim students only. In a region with substantial non-Muslim indigenous communities that is a real limit, though it follows from what a madrasah is; it is stated here because the bill states it and a reader should not have to infer it.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 167, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
Where Bill 167 pays for madrasah education as it exists, this one proposes to rebuild the curriculum underneath it.

The bill creates a Special Madrasah Fund to review, redesign, pilot test and then implement a balanced basic madrasah curriculum from Grade 1 to Senior High School. "Balanced" is the operative word and the text defines it at length: curricula that are interactively balanced for the spiritual and worldly development of the learner, that integrate the core subjects of mainstream basic education in deeply contextualised form, and that guarantee parallelism with — the text says if not superiority to — what DepEd prescribes for standard madaris.

The method is set out as a sequence. Existing curricula and textbooks are reviewed and redesigned; a Project Management Team merges related subjects to cut what the bill calls information overload; the result is field-tested in at least two qualified madaris for elementary and two for secondary in each province and in the Special Geographic Area; it is enhanced on the results, adopted in transition elsewhere for terminal validation, packaged, and then implemented by at least one madrasah for each level in every municipality and city in the region.

Governance sits with a Special Madrasah Fund Board chaired by the Directorate General for Madaris Education, with the Directorate Generals for Basic and Technical Education as associate chairpersons, and members drawn from the most prominent regional madaris association, the dominant registered ulama federation, and the regional offices of DepEd, TESDA, the Commission on Muslim Filipinos and the finance ministry. The Chief Minister appoints them for three years and may revoke an appointment for disgraceful or immoral conduct or corrupt practice. Board membership must be balanced across expertise in Islamic scholarship, curriculum development, school management, and fund administration.

The destination is accreditation. The bill’s stated ultimate goal is that DepEd recognize the madrasah as a Standard Muslim Education Institution and issue Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificates, so a madrasah completer can transfer into the state system, enrol at the next level, or present the certificate as an educational qualification for a job.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note makes an argument few filed bills bother with. It says the balanced madrasah is idealised and does not exist: the madaris DepEd accredits as Standard Private Madrasah are balanced only in the sense that five core subjects have been added on top of the Qur’an, Seerah, Hadith, Aqeedah, Fiqh and Arabic, which produces information overload rather than integration. It cites the Constitution’s education article and Section 16 of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, and it argues its theological case from Surah Al-Qasas 28:77 and a hadith on not surrendering either world for the other.

The practical driver is the Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificate. Without it, years spent in a madrasah convert into nothing a state school or an employer will count.
whoIsAffected: Madrasah learners from Grade 1 to Senior High School, whose curriculum and textbooks would be rewritten.
Madrasah completers, for whom the accreditation certificate would convert years of study into a recognized qualification.
The madaris selected for pilot testing — at least 2 for elementary and 2 for secondary in each province and in the Special Geographic Area — and eventually at least one per municipality or city.
Gurus, who would teach a merged and rewritten subject set.
DepEd and TESDA, whose recognition the whole design depends on and who sit on the board.
The regional madaris association and the ulama federation, given seats on the board that governs the fund.
implementedBy: Special Madrasah Fund Board, chaired by the Directorate General for Madaris Education with the Directorate Generals for Basic Education and Technical Education as associate chairpersons, appointed by the Chief Minister for 3 years
A Project Management Team, recruited by the Board and approved by the MBHTE Minister, which prepares a 10-year development and operational plan and runs the review, rewriting and pilot testing
Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education
Department of Education, whose accreditation and equivalency certificate is the stated end point, in collaboration with MBHTE

funding.detail: No total is stated. Initial implementation is charged against the current year’s Bangsamoro appropriations and later years go into the annual General Appropriations Act. The bill does itemise what the money is for, which is more than most: curriculum and textbook review and development, reproduction of new textbooks, pilot testing in each province and the Special Geographic Area, and construction of pilot testing building units, specified as a 7-room unit of one office and six classrooms.

whatChanges: A standing fund exists to redesign the basic madrasah curriculum from Grade 1 to Senior High School.
Subjects are merged to reduce overload, and mainstream core subjects are integrated in contextualised form.
A board seating madaris and ulama organizations alongside DepEd, TESDA and the finance ministry governs the fund.
A 10-year development and operational plan is required, with budget allocations attached.
Curricula are pilot tested province by province before general adoption, then rolled out to at least one madrasah per level per municipality or city.
Buildings are funded for the pilot sites, at a specified 7-room configuration.
readings.insight:
The whole design turns on something the Bangsamoro Parliament cannot legislate. The Learning Accreditation and Equivalency certificate is issued by DepEd, a national department, and the bill can fund the curriculum, staff the board and run the pilots but cannot make DepEd recognize the result. The text is careful about this — it says the measure creates the "potentiality" that DepEd would accredit, and that the mechanics are for the Department to set in collaboration with MBHTE. That is honest drafting, and it also means the bill’s stated ultimate goal is an outcome it can only make more likely.

The appropriations clause has aged. It names the provinces where pilot testing is to happen and the list includes Sulu, which the Supreme Court removed from the Bangsamoro in 2024, after this bill was filed in May 2023. Section 5, which sets out the same pilot design, refers instead to "every province of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region" and the Special Geographic Area — wording that survives the change. The two clauses now describe different maps.

One more thing worth noticing: the board seats are drawn from the "most prominent" regional madaris association and the "most dominant" registered ulama federation. Neither superlative is defined, and in a region with several competing ulama bodies, deciding which one is dominant is a political act the bill hands to whoever makes the appointment.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 168, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city of the region.

The interior ministry develops the criteria, qualifications and disqualifications. The award is called the "Best Lupong Tagapamayapa", and it carries 3 things: a commemorative plaque or medal; a monetary grant of ₱30,000, which may be increased as circumstances warrant; and an invitation to regional events that salute the importance of the barangay justice system.

There is 1 recipient in each municipality and city, annually. The ministry has 90 days to develop the programme and the rules governing selection.
readings.whyProposed:
A Lupong Tagapamayapa is unpaid. Its members mediate neighbours' disputes, land quarrels and family conflicts in their own time, and the measure of their success is a case that never becomes a court docket — which is invisible by definition.

Recognition and a modest grant are the only levers available for work that cannot be compensated as employment, and the bill's premise is that a Lupon that knows its work is noticed does it better.
whoIsAffected: Members of the Lupong Tagapamayapa in every barangay, who do this work unpaid.
The winning Lupon in each municipality and city, which receives ₱30,000 a year.
Communities whose disputes are mediated rather than litigated.
The Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, which sets the criteria and runs the selection.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government — criteria, qualifications and disqualifications, the programme, and the rules governing selection within 90 days

funding.detail: ₱30,000 per award, 1 in each municipality and city annually. With 116 municipalities and 3 cities in the region, the annual commitment at that rate is roughly ₱3.6 million — one of the few measures in this registry whose cost can be calculated from its own text.

whatChanges: The best Lupon in every municipality and city receives recognition and ₱30,000 a year.
The interior ministry must define what good barangay mediation looks like, in published criteria.
Lupon members are invited to regional events rather than remaining invisible.
readings.insight:
The criteria are the whole bill, and the bill delegates them. Deciding what makes a Lupong Tagapamayapa the best in its municipality means deciding what barangay justice is for — the number of disputes settled, the proportion that stay settled, the speed, the absence of complaints, or the willingness of parties to come back. Each of those rewards different behaviour, and a Lupon chasing settlement counts has an incentive to pressure a weaker party into agreeing. The interior ministry will write those criteria, and the published result will say more about the region's justice policy than this bill does.

The ₱30,000 is well calibrated for what it is. Too small to attract people who want money, large enough to matter to an unpaid panel in a rural barangay — it buys a filing cabinet, a meeting space, transport to hearings. The bill's provision that the grant may be increased as circumstances warrant is sensible drafting for a figure that will erode.

The Katarungang Pambarangay is the barangay justice system — the Lupong Tagapamayapa, a panel of community members that mediates disputes before they reach a court, and through which most Filipinos who encounter the justice system encounter it. In this region it also runs alongside Shari'ah courts and, under BAA 64, the customary justice systems of indigenous communities, so the barangay panel is 1 of 3 bodies a dispute might go to.

What the award scheme cannot do is address capacity, and the companion bills are the author's acknowledgment of that. A Lupon that does not know the law cannot apply it well no matter how it is incentivised, which is what Bill No. 172's handbook is for; and a Lupon with no standing in the local power structure cannot enforce a settlement, which is what Bill No. 173's federation and peace-and-order-council seats are for. Read alone this is a prize. Read as 1 of three, it is the recognition layer of a capacity programme.

MP Loong filed 3 bills on the barangay justice system together: Bill No. 170 creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city, Bill No. 172 requires a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook translated into the region's major languages, and Bill No. 173 federates the Lupon members and seats their presidents on the peace and order councils. All 3 remain at First Reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires the interior ministry to formulate, develop and publish a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook, translated into the major languages of the region.

Section 5 sets the standard the handbook must meet, and it is written in plain terms: the material must communicate the ideas clearly to the officials concerned, make the task of following the procedure as effortless as possible, and include annotations of the relevant laws — the Katarungang Pambarangay law, the jurisdictional rules, and special laws. It may be republished every 5 years to keep pace with new measures.

Section 6 handles distribution. The ministry provides an electronic and a hard copy to every barangay in the region, and requires each to keep a hard copy available in its office.

The implementing rules are drawn up in consultation with government agencies, experts, teachers, historians, linguists, legal luminaries and other stakeholders. The Act is titled the "Alay sa Lupon Act" — an offering to the Lupon.
readings.whyProposed:
The barangay justice system runs on unpaid volunteers applying procedural rules about jurisdiction, mediation, conciliation and the certification that allows a case to proceed to court. Getting those rules wrong means a settlement that will not hold or a case dismissed for want of the right certificate.

The handbook is the cheapest intervention available. It does not change the law, create a body or appropriate a facility — it puts the procedure in the hands of the people expected to follow it, in a language they read.
whoIsAffected: Lupong Tagapamayapa members in every barangay, who must apply procedural rules without legal training.
Parties to barangay disputes, whose settlements depend on the procedure being followed correctly.
Speakers of the region's major languages, into which the handbook must be translated.
Barangay offices, each required to keep a hard copy available.
Linguists, teachers and legal practitioners consulted on the implementing rules.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government — formulating, publishing, translating and distributing the handbook, and the implementing rules within 90 days in consultation with experts, teachers, historians, linguists and legal practitioners

funding.detail: No amount is named. The cost is translation, publication and distribution of a hard and electronic copy to every barangay in the region — a one-off with a 5-year republication cycle, and among the smallest price tags attached to any measure in this registry.

whatChanges: Every barangay receives a handbook on the justice system it is required to operate.
That handbook exists in the region's major languages, not only in English or Filipino.
A hard copy must be kept available in each barangay office.
The text is annotated with the relevant laws and republished every 5 years.
readings.insight:
Translation into the major languages is the provision that makes this bill worth more than its cost. The region's barangay officials work in Maranao, Maguindanaon, Tausug, Yakan, Sama and several others; the Katarungang Pambarangay law and its jurisprudence exist in English. A volunteer mediator reading procedural rules in a second or third language applies them approximately, and the resulting defect surfaces later as a settlement that will not stand or a case thrown out. This is the same instinct as the enacted BAA 59's requirement that agricultural training materials be delivered "in the language most appropriate to the end-user", and the Local Governance Code's provision for sessions in a local language with translated minutes — the region keeps returning to the point that a rule nobody can read is not in force.

Requiring both an electronic and a hard copy, with the hard copy kept available in the office, is unglamorous and correct. Barangay offices in much of this region have intermittent power and no reliable connection, and an electronic-only handbook would be a handbook nobody opens.

The 5-year republication cycle is the provision most likely to lapse. Statutes requiring periodic revision are routinely complied with once; the registry's own evidence is the Bangsamoro Register of Ordinances, which BAA 49 requires to be digital, online and public, and whose maintenance depends on the same ministry this bill relies on.

The Katarungang Pambarangay is the barangay justice system — the Lupong Tagapamayapa, a panel of community members that mediates disputes before they reach a court, and through which most Filipinos who encounter the justice system encounter it. In this region it also runs alongside Shari'ah courts and, under BAA 64, the customary justice systems of indigenous communities, so the barangay panel is 1 of 3 bodies a dispute might go to.

What makes the handbook harder than it looks is that in this region the barangay panel is not the only forum. A dispute between Muslims may belong before a Shari'ah court; one involving an indigenous community is governed, under BAA 64, by that community's customary law, with ambiguity resolved in its favour. A handbook on jurisdiction has to explain when the Lupon should not take a case at all, and the bill's instruction to include "jurisdictions" among the annotations is where that work would have to be done.

MP Loong filed 3 bills on the barangay justice system together: Bill No. 170 creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city, Bill No. 172 requires a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook translated into the region's major languages, and Bill No. 173 federates the Lupon members and seats their presidents on the peace and order councils. All 3 remain at First Reading.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 172, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This is the structural measure of the 3 — it federates the region's Lupong Tagapamayapa members and gives them a seat at the table where local security is decided.

A Federation of Lupong Tagapamayapa Members is created, with every barangay represented and chapters organised at municipal, city and provincial level, topped by a Regional Council. The interior ministry facilitates the election of the federation heads at each level.

Section 7 is the provision with real consequence. The elected presidents of the Federation at municipal, city and provincial level, and the chairperson of the Regional Council, serve as ex-officio members of the corresponding Peace and Order Council — municipal, city, provincial and regional. They hold those seats only while they hold the federation office, and in no case beyond the term of the government head who convened the council.

Section 9 funds the Federations from contributions by member local government units, from the regional government, and from their own fund-raising, with fund-raising proceeds tied to the projects they were raised for. Section 10 requires a Barangay Justice Summit within 6 months of the Federation being constituted. The Act is titled the "Enhanced Bangsamoro Barangay Justice" measure, and it cites Section 411 of the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code on the composition of the Lupong Tagapamayapa.
readings.whyProposed:
The barangay justice system handles an enormous share of the region's disputes and has no voice above the barangay. Lupon members are appointed locally, serve unpaid, and have no standing body through which to raise a problem, share practice or be consulted on policy that affects them.

Federating them creates that voice. Seating their presidents on the peace and order councils then connects the people who mediate disputes to the bodies that handle the consequences when mediation fails — which in this region means the councils that deal with rido, with armed incidents and with displacement.
whoIsAffected: Lupong Tagapamayapa members in every barangay, who gain a federation and representation above the barangay.
Municipal, city, provincial and regional Peace and Order Councils, which gain an ex-officio member from the barangay justice system.
Local government units, asked to contribute to the Federations' funds.
Communities affected by clan feuding, where mediation and peace-and-order responses meet.
The Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, which facilitates the federation elections.
implementedBy: A Federation of Lupong Tagapamayapa Members, with municipal, city and provincial chapters and a Regional Council
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, facilitating the election of federation heads at each level
Peace and Order Councils at municipal, city, provincial and regional level, which seat the federation presidents ex officio
A Barangay Justice Summit, within 6 months of the Federation being constituted

funding.detail: The Federations derive funds from contributions of member local government units, from the regional government, and from their own fund-raising, with fund-raising proceeds restricted to the projects they were raised for. No amount is named from any of the 3 sources, which leaves the Federation's capacity dependent on voluntary local contributions.

whatChanges: Lupon members are federated from barangay to regional level.
Federation presidents sit ex officio on the Peace and Order Councils at every level.
A Barangay Justice Summit convenes within 6 months.
The Federations may raise their own funds, restricted to the purposes raised for.
readings.insight:
Section 7 is the reason this is the most consequential of the 3 bills. Peace and Order Councils in this region are where armed incidents, clan feuding and displacement are handled, and their membership is officials and uniformed services. Putting the president of the barangay mediators' federation in the room as of right brings the one body that deals with disputes before they become violence into the body that deals with them after. For a region whose own legislation repeatedly identifies rido as a cause of displacement on a par with armed conflict, that is a structural connection worth making.

The term limitation attached to it is careful drafting. The seat lasts only while the person holds the federation office and in no case beyond the term of the government head who convened the council, which prevents a federation president outlasting the body they sit on and keeps the seat institutional rather than personal.

The funding is the weakness, and it is the familiar one. A federation funded by contributions from member local governments, an unquantified share from the regional government, and its own fund-raising has no assured income — and a body of unpaid volunteers running fund-raising projects to finance its own representation is a thin foundation for something the Act seats on 4 tiers of peace and order council. Compare the registry's other federated structure: the Local Governance Code enacted as BAA 49 provides insurance for the barangay tanod, a named benefit funded through the ordinary budget.

The Katarungang Pambarangay is the barangay justice system — the Lupong Tagapamayapa, a panel of community members that mediates disputes before they reach a court, and through which most Filipinos who encounter the justice system encounter it. In this region it also runs alongside Shari'ah courts and, under BAA 64, the customary justice systems of indigenous communities, so the barangay panel is 1 of 3 bodies a dispute might go to.

Citing Section 411 of the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code is worth noting because of the timing. That Code was enacted as BAA 49 in November 2023, and this bill was filed in April 2023 — so the citation is to a bill that had not yet become law when this measure was written. The 2 moved at very different speeds: the Code passed inside a year and this bill has never left First Reading.

MP Loong filed 3 bills on the barangay justice system together: Bill No. 170 creates an annual award for the best Lupong Tagapamayapa in every municipality and city, Bill No. 172 requires a Katarungang Pambarangay handbook translated into the region's major languages, and Bill No. 173 federates the Lupon members and seats their presidents on the peace and order councils. All 3 remain at First Reading.

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates, in every barangay of every city and municipality, a Barangay Justice System Multi-Sectoral Traditional and Customary Laws Advisory Council — a body to advise the barangay justice system on the customary law of the community it is settling disputes in.

The Council is chaired by the city or municipal mayor and seats a representative of the city or municipal police office, a purok leader, a traditional leader, a religious leader, an indigenous people’s leader, a tribal leader, and representatives of women, youth and persons with disabilities, each drawn from the barangay concerned.

Its functions are advisory and expressly without prejudice to the Katarungang Pambarangay Law, the national barangay justice statute. It provides specialised information, skills and experience on the community’s existing traditional and customary laws to aid the people running the barangay justice system; provides guidance and technical advice in areas outside the Lupon members’ usual expertise; encourages retirees from government and the private sector to join the barangay justice system; supplies customary and traditional laws that have fallen out of use through non-practice; and acts as the system’s advocate in the barangay.

Mayors must convene the Councils within 6 months of approval. Members receive no remuneration.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section is short and states the aim: that the customs, beliefs and traditions of the Bangsamoro people are recognized, respected and guaranteed, and that disputes are resolved justly and peacefully.

The practical case is that the Lupong Tagapamayapa — the barangay conciliation panel under national law — applies a national framework in communities whose disputes are actually governed by customary law, whether Moro or indigenous. The Council is meant to put that knowledge at the panel’s disposal rather than leave it to whichever member happens to have it.
whoIsAffected: Parties to barangay-level disputes, whose settlement would draw on customary law explicitly.
Lupong Tagapamayapa members, who gain an advisory body for matters outside their expertise.
Traditional, religious, indigenous and tribal leaders, given a formal role in the barangay justice system.
Women, youth and persons with disabilities, each given a seat.
City and municipal mayors, who chair every one of these Councils in their jurisdiction and must convene them within 6 months.
implementedBy: City and municipal mayors, as chairs and as the officials required to convene the Councils
The Councils themselves, in every barangay
City and municipal police offices, which supply a representative to each

funding.detail: The bill makes no appropriation and states that members receive no remuneration for their duties. It is designed to cost nothing, which is a defensible choice for an advisory body — and also the reason to ask how often bodies with no budget and no paid members actually meet.

whatChanges: Every barangay in the region gains a customary law advisory council for its justice system.
Traditional, religious, indigenous and tribal leaders acquire a formal advisory role.
Women, youth and PWD representatives sit on the council by right.
Customary laws that have fallen out of use through non-practice are to be supplied back to the system.
Mayors must convene the councils within 6 months of approval.
The Katarungang Pambarangay Law is expressly unaffected.
readings.insight:
The chairmanship does not scale, and it is the first thing a committee should look at. The Council exists in every barangay, and the chair of every one of them is the city or municipal mayor. Lanao del Sur has municipalities with dozens of barangays; a mayor there would chair dozens of separate councils. The bill gives no provision for a designated representative, no quorum rule, and no meeting schedule. As drafted, the person who must sit at the head of each council is the one person in the municipality who cannot be in all of them.

The function about disused customary law is the most interesting line in the bill and the least noticed. Providing the barangay justice system with "customary and traditional laws that may not have been in use for reasons of non-practice" is a revival mandate, not merely an advisory one — it invites councils to bring back rules that fell out of use. Whether that is restoration or invention will depend entirely on who sits on the council, which is why the composition matters as much as it does.

The seats for women, youth and persons with disabilities are worth noting for what they do in this context. Customary dispute resolution in the region is, in practice, largely conducted by senior men. Writing those three seats into the statute is a deliberate correction, and it sits in tension with the traditional and tribal leadership seats beside it in a way the bill leaves unresolved.

Read alongside Bill 159, which builds a whole PASAD office structure for alternative dispute resolution, this is the same instinct at a fraction of the cost — and both are before the Committee on the Bangsamoro Justice System.

readings.whatItDoes:
This sets out how to behave while the Bangsamoro Hymn is played, and then declines to punish anyone who does not.

The code has 7 rules. Stand at attention, upright, facing the Bangsamoro flag if one is displayed. Face the flag, or the direction of the sound if the hymn is pre-recorded, or the singer if the singer is visible. Place the right hand as a **closed fist** across the chest — and the bill is explicit that this applies to everyone, including those who cannot stand unaided, and that a person walking when the hymn begins must stop, stand at attention and hold the gesture until it ends. Remove the hat with the right hand and hold it against the chest, a protocol applying to men, women, children and the elderly — but expressly excluding any religious or culture-related headwear. Men in uniform salute from the first note and hold it to the last. Put away technological devices and give the hymn full attention. And do not applaud afterwards.

Coverage extends to all citizens and guests present, with ministries, government offices, agencies, educational institutions public and private, local government units and government corporations in the region "highly enjoined" to observe it.

Section 5 then states the consequence of breach: no punishment will be enforced for breaching the flag or hymn code of decorum, but it is imperative to respect the Mujahideen and Mujahidat who fought for the aspirations of the Bangsamoro people and to honour the region's symbols by observing it. The interior ministry and the education ministry write the rules within 90 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill grounds itself in Article II Section 2 of the Organic Law, the provision under which the region adopts its own flag, anthem and other symbols — the same authority BAA 1 used to adopt the flag.

What it is for is the gap that follows. A region that has legislated a flag and a hymn has said nothing about how either is to be treated, and in the absence of a rule, practice drifts toward whatever people remember of national anthem etiquette. Writing the code down fixes it, and Section 5 explains why the bill declines to enforce it: the reason for standing is respect for the people who fought, and respect compelled by penalty is a different thing.
whoIsAffected: Everyone present when the hymn is played, citizens and guests alike.
All ministries, government offices, agencies, local government units and government corporations in the region.
Public and private educational institutions, where the hymn is most often sung.
People who cannot stand unaided, expressly covered by the hand gesture rather than excused from the code.
Anyone wearing religious or cultural headwear, expressly exempted from the removal protocol.
Men in uniform, required to salute for the hymn's full duration.
implementedBy: Ministry of the Interior and Local Government, in coordination with the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education — implementing rules within 90 days

funding.detail: No appropriation and no penalty. The Act creates duties of observance and expressly provides that no punishment will be enforced for breaching them.

whatChanges: The region acquires a written code of decorum for its own hymn.
The gesture is a closed fist over the chest, and it applies to those who cannot stand as well as those who can.
Religious and cultural headwear is exempt from the requirement to uncover.
Applause after the hymn is declared improper.
Observance is required of every government office and school, and enforced against nobody.
readings.insight:
The closed fist is the whole bill in one gesture. Philippine national anthem etiquette, set by the national flag and heraldic code, is an open right palm over the heart; this bill specifies a closed fist. Nothing in the text explains the change, and none is needed — a clenched hand over the chest is the posture of a movement rather than of a citizenry, and the region is legislating decorum for a hymn about, as Section 4.7 puts it, "the Bangsamoro people's number one core value: the right to self-determination". Two symbols, 2 gestures, and the difference between them is the point.

The headwear exemption is the most carefully considered line in the document. A general rule requiring hats to be removed would collide immediately with the hijab, the kufi and the tubao, and a code drafted without noticing that would have made observance impossible for most of the people expected to observe it. Excluding religious and culture-related headwear from the protocol, while keeping it for ordinary hats, resolves that in a single clause.

So does the provision on people who cannot stand. Rather than excusing them, the bill extends the hand gesture to them expressly — "applies to everyone including those who cannot stand on their own". That is a small piece of drafting with a clear instinct behind it: a code of respect that writes disabled people out of the act of respect would be a worse code.

Section 5 is the bill's real argument and the reason it is not a trivial measure. It sets out obligations in detail and then states that no punishment will be enforced for breaching them, resting instead on what is owed to the people who fought. Anthem laws elsewhere commonly carry fines, and several countries prosecute people for sitting down. A region emerging from armed conflict, writing its first code of decorum for its own hymn, choosing to make it unenforceable is a deliberate decision about what its symbols are for — and it is the opposite of the choice most governments make.

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires all signage in the Bangsamoro, in both public and private institutions and establishments, to be in English and Arabic.

The two must appear together — written side by side, or English above and Arabic below. Signage is defined broadly: any written announcement installed, posted, hung, painted or otherwise displayed in a public place, and generally any graphic display intended to convey information to an audience. The Ministry of Public Works is to provide a list of all appropriate and lawful signages and other devices and instruments.

Funds come from the Bangsamoro appropriations act. The Act takes effect 15 days after publication in at least two newspapers of regional circulation.
readings.whyProposed:
The declaration of policy states it as inclusivity: the Bangsamoro Government respects and promotes inclusivity within the region, and to that end mandates English-Arabic signage in public and private establishments.

Arabic is the liturgical language of Islam and the language of madrasah instruction across the region, and its visible presence in public space is a marker of the Bangsamoro identity the autonomy arrangement exists to express.
whoIsAffected: Every private establishment in the region — shops, restaurants, offices, clinics — which would have to replace or supplement its signage.
Every public institution and government office in the region.
The Ministry of Public Works, which must issue the list of appropriate and lawful signages.
Readers of Arabic, for whom public information becomes accessible.
Speakers of the region’s own languages — Maguindanaon, Maranao, Tausug, Sinama, Yakan, Iranun — and of Filipino, none of which the bill provides for.
implementedBy: Ministry of Public Works (MPW), which provides the list of appropriate and lawful signages, devices and instruments

funding.detail: No figure. Funds are charged against the General Appropriation Act of the Bangsamoro. The appropriation would cover government signage; the bill also binds every private establishment in the region and says nothing about who pays for theirs, which is the larger cost by far and falls on the businesses.

whatChanges: All signage in the region, public and private, must be in English and Arabic.
The two languages must appear together — side by side, or English above Arabic.
MPW must publish a list of appropriate and lawful signages.
Government signage costs come from the Bangsamoro appropriations act.
readings.insight:
Section 4 defines "Official Language" as "English-Arabic, to be used in signages" — and that definition is where the difficulty is. Under the Constitution the national language is Filipino, and the official languages are Filipino and English. The Bangsamoro Organic Law treats Arabic as an official language of the region alongside Filipino and English, so Arabic on public signage is on solid ground; what is not is a signage rule that requires English and Arabic and leaves Filipino out entirely.

The compliance cost is the second thing, and it is not small. The bill binds every private establishment in the region and provides money only through the regional appropriations act, which will not be paying for the signage of shops in Bongao or Marawi. Nor is there a transition period, a threshold exempting small businesses, or a penalty — so the Act takes effect 15 days after publication and every non-compliant sign in the region is immediately non-compliant with no stated consequence, which is a strange combination.

Third, and most substantively: the region has six or more living languages of its own. A signage law justified by inclusivity that mandates Arabic and English while making no provision for Maguindanaon, Maranao, Tausug, Sinama, Yakan or Iranun is making a particular argument about what Bangsamoro identity consists of. That is a legitimate argument to make and the bill should be read as making it.

It carries 9 principal authors, among the most in this batch, which suggests the argument is widely shared.

readings.whatItDoes:
Eight articles and 2 pages. This directs the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage to establish a Mujahideen Memorial Wall in the region, carrying a list of the names of certified Moro Islamic Liberation Front and Moro National Liberation Front members who died in the struggle for the right to self-determination.

Article 4 creates a Committee of 5 members appointed by the Chief Minister, whose single task is to establish the eligibility criteria for standard verification in identifying the Mujahideen, and to give the heritage commission the final list of names for inclusion.

Funds come from the general appropriations of the Bangsamoro. The bill names no site, no dimensions, no design and no deadline.
readings.whyProposed:
The authority cited is Section 24 of Article IX of the Organic Law — the Bangsamoro Government's duty to preserve the history, culture, arts, traditions and rich cultural heritage of the Bangsamoro people.

The measure's purpose is to put the dead of both fronts on a single wall. The MNLF and the MILF fought the same war in different decades and signed separate agreements with the national government, and a memorial that names members of both is a statement that the struggle was one struggle.
whoIsAffected: Families of MNLF and MILF members who died in the conflict, whose relatives' names may appear.
Families whose relatives are not certified, who have no route to inclusion that the bill describes.
The Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which must build and hold the Wall.
A 5-member Committee appointed by the Chief Minister, which sets who counts as Mujahideen.
Both former fronts, whose dead are commemorated together on one monument.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, which establishes the Wall
A Committee of 5 appointed by the Chief Minister, which sets the eligibility criteria and supplies the final list of names

funding.detail: No amount is named; the funds necessary are charged against the general appropriations of the Bangsamoro. For comparison, the 2 commemorative measures that became law in this registry carry figures — BAA 61 appropriates ₱15 million for the Camp Abubakar memorial and eco-park, and BAA 60 ₱5 million for the Hashim and Mimbantas memorial site.

whatChanges: The region would acquire a single memorial naming the dead of both the MNLF and the MILF.
A committee would fix, for the first time, the criteria for who counts as a Mujahideen who died in the struggle.
The heritage commission takes on a third commemorative site.
readings.insight:
The committee is the whole bill, and the bill does not notice it. Five people appointed by the Chief Minister would decide the eligibility criteria for who counts among the dead of a 5-decade armed struggle, and then supply the final list of names. There is no appeal, no grievance mechanism, no requirement to consult the families, and no standard the criteria must meet — the Act delegates the question entirely and says nothing about how it should be answered.

That gap is the more striking because Parliament had already addressed it. BAA 61, the Camp Abubakar memorial act, requires its management board to keep a functioning grievance mechanism and to consult and actively involve local communities, precisely because the hardest question in a memorial is whose names go on it. BAA 60 seats a representative of each family on the board governing the site where their relatives are buried. This bill, filed in May 2023 between those 2 measures, carries neither.

The word "certified" is where the difficulty concentrates. Certification implies a record, and the registry shows what records exist: the veteran mujahideen bills establish that determining who served, and for how long, requires asking the MILF and MNLF Central Committees, because the fronts kept the only lists there are. So the committee's criteria will in practice be applied to names supplied by the organisations whose dead are being commemorated — which is unavoidable and worth stating, since it means the state is ratifying a list rather than compiling one.

Commemorating both fronts on 1 wall is the bill's substantive contribution and it is not a small one. The MNLF signed in 1996 and the MILF in 2014, and the relationship between them has not always been easy. A monument that does not distinguish between their dead is a political act in the direction of a single Bangsamoro history, and it is the only measure in this registry that treats the 2 movements as one.
