readings.whatItDoes:
This converts the Upi Agricultural School in Upi, Maguindanao del Norte, into the Bangsamoro Tribal University.

The mandate is broad: advanced studies, higher professional and technical instruction and training, basic education for special purposes, research and extension services, and progressive leadership in education, arts, agriculture, environmental and technological development. And one element the others do not have — it is to integrate and offer studies on the culture of the people, specifically the indigenous peoples of the region.

Curricular offerings run to graduate, undergraduate, technical and short-term courses in agriculture, education, indigenous peoples culture, arts and sciences, as the Board of Trustees deems necessary to meet the needs of Maguindanao del Norte and the region.

The University holds the general powers of a corporation, governed by a Board of Trustees with enumerated powers and duties, meeting at least once a period, with administration vested in a University President.
readings.whyProposed:
A tribal university has been the region's declared policy since 2021 and has never been chartered. BAA 18, the education code, lists a Tribal University System among the provisions for indigenous learners. BAA 64, the indigenous peoples act of 2024, directs that the Tribal University be open to all regardless of religion, ethnicity or nationality while prioritising indigenous learners. Bill No. 47, the education reorganisation measure, directs Parliament to create a tribal university system.

Three instruments assume the institution exists or will. This bill is the one that would actually create it, and it does so by converting a school that already operates in Teduray country rather than by building something new.
whoIsAffected: Non-Moro indigenous learners — Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo and others — for whom the institution is primarily intended.
Students of the existing Upi Agricultural School, whose school becomes a university.
Upi and South Upi, where the Teduray population concentrates and where the school sits.
Maguindanao del Norte, whose needs the curricular offerings must meet.
Anyone studying indigenous peoples culture, which becomes a degree subject rather than a module.
implementedBy: Bangsamoro Tribal University, holding the general powers of a corporation
A Board of Trustees with enumerated powers and duties
A University President, in whom administration is vested

funding.detail: The bill converts an existing school rather than building a new institution, so the starting point is the Upi Agricultural School's own establishment and budget. A university offering graduate programmes needs considerably more than a secondary agricultural school, and the filed copy leaves the figure to the appropriations act.

whatChanges: The region finally gets the tribal university its own laws have assumed since 2021.
Indigenous peoples culture becomes a field of degree study.
An agricultural secondary school becomes a degree-granting institution with a graduate programme.
Upi acquires a university in the part of the region with the largest non-Moro indigenous population.
readings.insight:
This is the charter for an institution the region has mandated twice and never created. BAA 18 provided for a Tribal University System in 2021; BAA 64 in 2024 legislated how the Tribal University must behave — open to all regardless of religion, ethnicity or nationality, prioritising indigenous learners — without the university existing. A statute regulating the admissions policy of a school that has no charter is the clearest evidence in this registry of the gap between what the region declares and what it establishes, and this bill, filed in January 2024 and still at Committee Stage, is the measure that would close it.

Siting it at Upi is the decision that makes it a tribal university rather than a university with a tribal name. Upi and South Upi are Teduray country — the South Upi hospital bill records that more than 70% of its patients are Teduray and that the hospital staff work in the Teduray language — so converting the school that is already there attaches the institution to the community it is for. Building a new campus in Cotabato City would have produced something different.

The drafting carries 1 clear slip. Section 1 converts the school "in to a college to be known as the Bangsamoro Tribal University". A college and a university are different things in Philippine higher education law, with different programme and faculty requirements, and the section names both for the same institution. Since the rest of the bill provides for graduate offerings, a Board of Trustees and a President, the intent is plainly a university, and the word "college" would have to go.

What the bill does not address is the relationship to the Kulliyyah. BAA 50 created the Bangsamoro Kulliyyah for Islamic Studies at Buluan with a chartered board, financial autonomy and a socialised tuition duty, and it was enacted in November 2023 — 2 months before this bill was filed. The region chartered its Islamic studies institution and has not chartered its tribal one, and the 2 measures are close enough in form that the comparison is unavoidable.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 274, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This grants government officials and employees 15 calendar days of Moral Recovery Leave, once in an entire career.

The entitlement is defined by belief rather than by faith: the leave goes to all officials and to regular and casual employees "who subscribe to a religion or belong to a faith or spiritual group". It is for taking part in, observing or practising religious, faith-based or spiritual traditions and activities that invigorate moral uprightness — and Section 4 names examples in both directions, pilgrimages, multi-day congregations and spiritual retreats, "such as the Umrah or Hajj pilgrimage for Muslims, and the pilgrimage to Jerusalem City or Vatican City for Christians".

Unused leave is not monetizable, which closes off the obvious way a one-time benefit turns into a cash entitlement. The Civil Service Commission writes the rules within 60 days of effectivity, and nothing in the Act may be read to reduce any existing benefit under any law, order or collective agreement.

Ten sections, 3 pages, and no appropriation clause.
readings.whyProposed:
The explanatory note runs the argument through moral governance, which it calls one of the guiding tenets of the Bangsamoro Government and a rallying call of its leadership — inscribed in the Bangsamoro Administrative Code as a government driven by dedication, devotion, honesty, justice and integrity, and devoid of graft and corruption.

The leave is presented as the personal and spiritual counterpart to that institutional commitment: a way of supplementing the inculcation of moral governance at the level of the individual employee. The note also anchors it in the national Moral Recovery Program and its formulation Maka-Diyos, Maka-Tao, Maka-Bayan at Maka-Kalikasan.

And it addresses the objection directly, in its own last paragraph: the Act "does not intend to favor any particular group or religion", and is meant as an accommodation for employees with diverse belief systems to exercise their religious freedom.
whoIsAffected: All Bangsamoro government officials and regular and casual employees who subscribe to a religion or belong to a faith or spiritual group.
Employees of no religious affiliation, who on the face of Section 3 are not entitled to it.
Muslim employees intending Umrah or Hajj, and Christian employees intending Jerusalem or the Vatican, both named in the text.
The Civil Service Commission, which writes the implementing rules within 60 days.
Heads of office, who must absorb the absence — the bill sets no operational escape clause.
implementedBy: Civil Service Commission — implementing rules and regulations within 60 days of effectivity

funding.detail: No appropriation clause. The cost sits wherever the employee's salary already sits, and unused leave may not be monetized.

whatChanges: Government employees gain 15 calendar days of leave for religious or spiritual observance, once in a career.
The entitlement is written to cover any faith or spiritual group, not one.
Unused leave cannot be converted to cash.
Existing leave benefits under any other law or agreement are expressly preserved.
readings.insight:
This bill and Bill No. 282 are 2 answers to the same question, filed 3 days apart, and Parliament took both — Committee Report No. 176 covers them jointly. Read side by side they disagree about nearly everything that matters. This one gives 15 days; the other gives 30. This one says nothing about pay; the other says paid. This one requires no length of service; the other requires 2 years. This one has the Civil Service Commission write rules and stops; the other routes every application to the Chief Minister, demands a written report afterwards, and threatens administrative sanctions against anyone who takes the leave and does not make the pilgrimage.

The drafting difference that matters most is the framing. Bill 282 is the Pilgrimage Leave Act and speaks of pilgrimage throughout. This one is the Moral Recovery Leave Act, defines the benefit by subscription to any religion, faith or spiritual group, and names a Christian pilgrimage alongside a Muslim one in the operative text rather than in the note. In a region with a Muslim majority, a Christian minority and indigenous communities whose practices fit neither category neatly, that choice decides who can claim the leave without having to argue for it. The one group Section 3 does leave out is employees who subscribe to nothing.

The calendar tells the rest. Filed 2 February 2024, First Reading on 26 February, then referred to committee in July and left there until the committee report was adopted on 19 November 2025. From that day the measure was deferred 17 times across 20 months — through January, April, May, June and July 2026 — before passing Third and Final Reading on 16 July 2026. Twenty-nine months for a 3-page bill granting leave.

A note on the act number, because the registry does not agree with itself. Parliament's bills index records this measure as becoming BAA 94. Parliament's acts index gives BAA 94 a completely different title — the Special Geographic Area Development Authority act — word for word identical to its own entry for BAA 93, both dated 16 July 2026. One of those 2 entries is wrong, and since the leave measure passed Third and Final Reading on that same date, the likeliest reading is that the acts index duplicated BAA 93 into the BAA 94 slot and lost the leave act. No PDF has been published for BAA 92, 93 or 94, so the enacted text cannot be checked against either index. What follows is the bill as filed, not the law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 276, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
This is a staffing and equipment bill for a single hospital, and it changes no bed count.

Republic Act No. 11330 converted the Dinaig Municipal Hospital into what is now the Datu Odin Sinsuat District Hospital. This measure requires the Bangsamoro Government, in consultation with the provincial government of Maguindanao del Norte, the health ministry and the hospital's own management, to do 2 things: provide the support, financial or otherwise, needed to staff the hospital adequately — with the required plantilla positions determined by the health ministry together with the finance ministry and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission — and provide the support needed to equip it with machines, equipment and facilities meeting the requirements of modern medical services and its status as a district hospital.

In return the hospital's management must report to the health ministry on its human resource gaps, its bed occupancy rate and other comprehensive information, and submit development plans consistent with its district-hospital status.
readings.whyProposed:
A national law gave this hospital a district-hospital designation. The designation did not bring staff or equipment, and the gap between the status and the reality is what the bill addresses.

Requiring reports on human resource gaps and bed occupancy is the mechanism. A hospital that must state its own shortfall annually creates the record on which an appropriation can be justified, which is what has been missing.
whoIsAffected: Patients of the Datu Odin Sinsuat District Hospital, in the most populous municipality of Maguindanao del Norte.
The hospital's staff, carrying a district-hospital designation without a district-hospital complement.
Applicants for the plantilla positions the health, finance and civil service bodies must determine.
The provincial government of Maguindanao del Norte, consulted on the support.
The Ministry of Health, which receives the reports on human resource gaps and bed occupancy.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, in coordination with the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Management and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission — determining the required plantilla positions
The hospital's own management, which must report human resource gaps, bed occupancy and development plans
The provincial government of Maguindanao del Norte, consulted throughout

funding.detail: No amount is named. The health ministry includes implementation in its programmes and the funding goes into the annual Bangsamoro appropriations law. Because the substance is permanent plantilla positions rather than a building, the commitment is recurring salary cost.

whatChanges: A hospital with a national district-hospital designation gets the staff and equipment to match it.
Plantilla positions are determined jointly by the health, finance and civil service bodies.
The hospital must report its human resource gaps and bed occupancy to the ministry.
The provincial government is brought into consultation on a regionally funded hospital.
readings.insight:
Two members filed bills about this same hospital a year apart and they do opposite halves of the job. Bill No. 146, filed by MP Anayatin in March 2023, raises the authorised capacity from 50 beds to 100 and documents that the 50-bed designation under Republic Act No. 11330 has run on a 10-bed budget in a building designed for 10 beds. This bill, filed by MP Dilangalen in February 2024, leaves the capacity alone and legislates the staffing and equipment for the designation the hospital already has.

Read together they are the sharper measure. Raising a designation that is not funded produces another unfunded designation; funding the existing one produces a working hospital. Neither bill mentions the other, and both are at Committee Stage.

The reporting duty is the provision most worth keeping. Requiring the hospital to state its human resource gaps and its bed occupancy rate turns the problem into a number that recurs annually in the ministry's files — and bed occupancy is exactly the figure that made the strongest hospital arguments in this registry, with South Upi documented at 136% to 362% and the Tawi-Tawi provincial hospital at 150 to 200%. A hospital that reports its own occupancy builds the case for its own staffing without anyone filing a bill.

This is the third measure in the registry whose entire subject is the gap between a hospital's designation and its staff — the others being Bill No. 189 for the Montaner hospital's 100-bed capacity and Bill No. 146 for this one. Three separate members identified the same structural failure and legislated against it in 3 separate bills, none of which has passed, while a dozen bills creating new hospital designations moved ahead of them.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 277, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This requires all provincial government tertiary hospitals in the region to establish, operate and maintain a dialysis ward or unit within 1 year of effectivity — adequately staffed and equipped with complete dialysis machines, equipment and supplies.

Dialysis is to be free to indigent patients in all provincial tertiary hospitals. Section 5 then sets out what a patient must produce to qualify: an Affidavit of Indigency, and a Certificate of Indigency from the national social welfare department or from the city or municipal social welfare office with jurisdiction over the patient's residence — or a Certificate of Indigency and/or No Income from the office of the Punong Barangay.

The health ministry issues the rules within 90 days, and funding comes from its current appropriations and then the annual appropriations act.
readings.whyProposed:
The bill takes the narrowest scope of the 3 dialysis measures and pairs it with the shortest deadline, which is a coherent judgement: provincial tertiary hospitals are the facilities that already have the theatre space, the specialists and the referral load to run a dialysis ward, and requiring it of them within a year is achievable in a way that requiring it of every government hospital is not.

The documentary provisions point to a second concern. Free treatment without a defined eligibility test invites either abuse or arbitrary refusal, and the bill's answer is to name exactly which papers establish indigency and which offices may issue them.
whoIsAffected: Kidney patients in the 5 provinces, who would have dialysis at their provincial tertiary hospital within a year.
Indigent patients, who receive free treatment on producing the named documents.
Patients unable to obtain an affidavit and certificate, who would pay.
Provincial government tertiary hospitals, which must build, staff and run a unit within 1 year.
Barangay chairpersons and municipal and city social welfare offices, which issue the certificates.
Patients at municipal and district hospitals, who fall outside the Act.
implementedBy: Provincial government tertiary hospitals, which establish, operate and maintain the units
Ministry of Health — implementing rules within 90 days
The national social welfare department, city and municipal social welfare offices, and barangay chairpersons, issuing certificates of indigency

funding.detail: No amount is named. Initial implementation is charged against the Ministry of Health's current appropriations, with continuing costs in the annual Bangsamoro appropriations act. A 1-year deadline to equip and staff dialysis wards in every provincial tertiary hospital, funded from an existing ministry line, is the same unfunded-mandate problem the other dialysis bills have, compressed into a fifth of the time.

whatChanges: Provincial tertiary hospitals must run dialysis wards within 1 year.
Dialysis becomes free for indigent patients at those hospitals.
Eligibility for free treatment is established by named documents from named offices.
readings.insight:
The documentary requirement is the provision to weigh, and it cuts both ways for the patient it is meant to help. Requiring an Affidavit of Indigency plus a certificate from the social welfare office or the barangay chairperson gives a hospital a clear rule and an indigent patient a defence against arbitrary refusal. It also puts 2 pieces of paper between a person in kidney failure and a treatment they need 2 or 3 times a week — an affidavit means finding someone to notarise it, and a certificate means a trip to an office that keeps its own hours. Bill No. 88 takes the other route entirely, having the social services ministry identify indigent patients rather than making them prove it.

The narrowing to provincial tertiary hospitals is this bill's strongest and weakest feature at once. It is realistic: those hospitals have the infrastructure, and a 1-year deadline against a handful of facilities is a deadline that could be met. It also leaves out everybody who cannot reach a provincial capital 3 times a week, which in Sulu and Tawi-Tawi is most of the population — and those are island provinces where the provincial hospital is itself across water from much of the province.

The 1-year deadline against an unnamed budget is the internal contradiction. Equipping and staffing a dialysis ward is a procurement and a recruitment, and 12 months is short for both even with money identified; funded "against the current appropriations of the MOH" it is a deadline the ministry cannot be held to. Of the 3 bills, only Bill No. 145 pairs its requirement with a figure, and it is the 1 that asks for the least.

Three bills in this registry address dialysis and they pick 3 different scales. Bill No. 88, filed by MP Mawallil in October 2022, requires a dialysis unit in every government hospital in the region within 5 years. Bill No. 145, filed by MP Sema in February 2023, builds 1 centre at 1 named hospital with ₱20 million behind it. Bill No. 279, filed by MP Dilangalen in February 2024, requires provincial tertiary hospitals to have a unit within 1 year. All 3 are at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and none has become law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 279, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This grants employees in both the private and public sectors 5 working days of bereavement leave at full pay on the death of an immediate family member — expressly "to grieve, attend to or make arrangements for the funeral".

Immediate family covers the employee's spouse, parents, child, brother or sister. The employer may request reasonable documentation, such as a death certificate or an obituary, to support the request.

Three provisions give the entitlement force. Section 4 provides that nothing in the Act reduces existing benefits under any law, order, contract, agreement or policy. Section 5 guarantees security of tenure: taking the leave may not be used as a reason for misconduct, demotion or termination, or treated as unsatisfactory performance. Section 6 sets a penalty — any person, corporation, trust, firm, partnership, association or entity violating the Act or its rules is fined up to ₱15,000, and where a corporate body is the violator, imprisonment falls on its responsible officers, including the president, vice president, chief officer, general manager, managing director or partner directly responsible.

The Ministry of Labor and Employment writes the rules for the private sector and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission for the public sector, each within 30 days.
readings.whyProposed:
The policy section makes the welfare case directly: the region's duty is to support employees at the point where a family death and the demands of work collide, and to make the time to grieve and to bury a relative an entitlement rather than a concession.

The drafting suggests a second concern. Naming security of tenure and attaching a penalty means the author expected the entitlement to be refused — which is the realistic expectation for a new leave benefit in an economy of small employers, and the reason the bill spends 3 of its 10 sections on making the leave safe to take.
whoIsAffected: All employees in the region, private and public sector.
Employees whose spouse dies, covered here and not in the companion bill.
Employers, who may ask for a death certificate or obituary but face a fine of up to ₱15,000 for refusing the leave.
Company officers — presidents, general managers, managing directors and partners — who face imprisonment where a corporate employer violates the Act.
Employees who fear retaliation, protected by an express security of tenure clause.
The Ministry of Labor and Employment and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission, writing rules for their respective sectors.
implementedBy: Ministry of Labor and Employment — implementing rules for the private sector within 30 days
Bangsamoro Civil Service Commission — implementing rules for the public sector within 30 days

funding.detail: No appropriation. The cost falls on employers as 5 working days of full pay per bereavement, and on the regional and local governments as employers of their own staff. The bill raises revenue only incidentally, through fines of up to ₱15,000 on employers who refuse.

whatChanges: Employees gain 5 working days of fully paid leave on the death of a spouse, parent, child or sibling.
Taking the leave cannot be treated as misconduct or grounds for demotion or dismissal.
Refusing the leave becomes an offence punishable by a fine, with imprisonment for responsible corporate officers.
Employers may require a death certificate or obituary but not more.
readings.insight:
Section 5 is the provision that makes this bill work, and it is the one its companion lacks. A statutory right to 5 days' leave means nothing to a contractual worker who believes taking it will cost them the job; saying in the Act that availment cannot be used as a reason for misconduct, demotion, termination or an unsatisfactory performance rating is what converts the entitlement into something a person will actually claim. Bill No. 270 grants the leave and says nothing about what happens to the employee who takes it.

The penalty structure is the other half of the same thought, and it is drafted with more care than the cash figure suggests. A fine capped at ₱15,000 is small against a large employer's payroll. But Section 6 also reaches the individuals — president, vice president, chief officer, general manager, managing director or the partner directly responsible — and personal exposure of named officers is a materially different deterrent from a corporate fine. The drafting does leave an oddity: the section states a fine as the penalty and then provides for imprisonment of officers where the violator is a corporation, without stating an imprisonment term anywhere.

Full pay for 5 working days, against the companion bill's 5 days at half pay, is the substantive policy difference, and this bill is the more expensive and the more coherent of the two. Bereavement leave exists because a grieving employee cannot work; paying half of it asks them to absorb part of the cost of their own bereavement. Whether the region's small establishments can carry the full version is a real question, and neither bill contains any estimate of what it would cost.

Requiring documentation is the small provision worth keeping from this version. A death certificate or an obituary is proof an employee can produce without difficulty, and naming those 2 examples in the statute forecloses an employer demanding something harder — while the companion bill's 2-day availment deadline achieves verification by making the benefit difficult to claim at all.

Two bereavement leave bills sit in this registry, filed 2 weeks apart in early 2024. Bill No. 270 is MP Sema's, granting 5 days at half pay; Bill No. 281 is MP Hashim's, granting 5 working days at full pay with a penalty for employers who refuse. Both are still at Second Reading, Committee Stage, and the region has no bereavement leave.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 281, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This grants Bangsamoro officials and employees 30 calendar days of paid leave to perform a pilgrimage, once in a lifetime.

Eligibility turns on service: an aggregate of 2 years with the Bangsamoro government qualifies, and the leave may be taken only once regardless of which office in the region the employee works in at the time of application. Pilgrimage is defined broadly — visiting a place of religious or spiritual importance to perform acts of worship or a spiritual journey — without naming any faith.

The approval chain is where this bill does its real work, and it runs to the top. The Chief Minister approves applications on the favorable recommendation of the head of office. Parliament's own staff go to the Speaker instead. Local government employees are recommended by their local chief executive and then sent to the Chief Minister through the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government. Every application reaches the Office of the Chief Minister, which keeps the record of everyone in the region who has taken the leave, local governments included. A head of office may refuse to recommend an application if granting it would seriously hamper operations.

Two provisions have no counterpart in the competing bill. Section 7 requires anyone who takes the leave to submit a written report on the pilgrimage they performed, within 30 days of returning to work. Section 8 makes an employee who deliberately did not perform the pilgrimage despite taking the leave subject to administrative sanctions and penalties.

The money goes in the budget of the Office of the Chief Minister, and that office and the Civil Service Commission jointly write the rules within 90 days.
readings.whyProposed:
There is no explanatory note attached to the filed copy. Section 2 states the policy in 2 sentences: the Bangsamoro Government exercises its powers to promote the general welfare, and it "realizes the role of a strong and contented workforce in achieving a developed Bangsamoro region".

That is a workforce argument rather than a religious one, and it is the only case the document makes for itself. The bill carries 29 co-authors on its face, which is the other thing it offers in place of a note.
whoIsAffected: Every Bangsamoro government official and employee with at least 2 years of aggregate service, including in local government units.
Employees with under 2 years of service, who do not qualify.
The Office of the Chief Minister, which approves every application in the region and keeps the central record.
The Speaker, who approves for Parliament's own officials and employees.
Local chief executives, who must recommend before an application can proceed.
Heads of office, who may refuse to recommend where the absence would seriously hamper operations.
Anyone who takes the leave, who must file a written report and may face sanctions for not making the pilgrimage.
implementedBy: Office of the Chief Minister — approval of every application, central record-keeping, receipt of post-leave reports, and the budget line
Office of the Parliament Speaker — approval for Parliament's own officials and employees
Ministry of the Interior and Local Government — the route by which local government applications reach the Chief Minister
Civil Service Commission for BARMM, jointly with the Office of the Chief Minister — implementing rules within 90 days

funding.detail: No amount is named. The cost is carried in the budget of the Office of the Chief Minister, with later requirements in the annual Bangsamoro Appropriations Act. Because the leave is paid and runs 30 calendar days, the appropriation is in substance a salary continuation for everyone who takes it.

whatChanges: Government employees with 2 years of service gain 30 calendar days of paid leave for pilgrimage, once in a lifetime.
The Chief Minister personally approves every such application in the region, including from local governments.
A central register of everyone who has taken the leave is kept in the Office of the Chief Minister.
Taking the leave creates a duty to report on the pilgrimage within 30 days of returning.
Not performing the pilgrimage after taking the leave becomes an administrative offense.
readings.insight:
Sections 7 and 8 are what distinguish this bill, and they are worth stating plainly: an employee who takes this leave must afterwards file a written account of their pilgrimage with the Office of the Chief Minister, and one who deliberately did not perform it faces administrative sanctions. The state is verifying an act of worship. There is a defensible reason — 30 days of paid absence is public money, and a benefit without a check invites the obvious abuse — but the check chosen puts a government office in the position of assessing whether someone's devotional journey really happened. The competing bill, which grants half the days and says nothing about pay, needs no such apparatus.

The approval chain compounds it. Every application in the region, from every ministry and every local government unit, lands on the Chief Minister's desk. For a benefit of this kind the natural approver is the employee's own agency head, and this bill makes that person a recommender only. What the design produces is a single regional register of which public servants have made a pilgrimage and when — a document that does not otherwise exist and that the bill does not say who may see.

Set against Bill No. 276, the 2 measures differ in nearly every parameter: 30 days against 15, paid against unstated, 2 years of service against none, a named approval chain against none, and a sanction against nothing. What they share is the vocabulary of accommodation, and where 276 writes religious neutrality into its operative text by naming both Muslim and Christian destinations, this one achieves neutrality by naming nothing at all — a pilgrimage is any journey to a place of religious or spiritual importance.

The path through Parliament was the same for both. Filed 5 February 2024, First Reading on 29 February, referred to the Committee on Rules in June 2024, and then nothing until Committee Report No. 176 took this bill and 276 together on 19 November 2025. Seventeen deferrals followed across 20 months before Third and Final Reading on 16 July 2026.

A note on the act number, because the registry does not agree with itself. Parliament's bills index records this measure as becoming BAA 94. Parliament's acts index gives BAA 94 a completely different title — the Special Geographic Area Development Authority act — word for word identical to its own entry for BAA 93, both dated 16 July 2026. One of those 2 entries is wrong, and since the leave measure passed Third and Final Reading on that same date, the likeliest reading is that the acts index duplicated BAA 93 into the BAA 94 slot and lost the leave act. No PDF has been published for BAA 92, 93 or 94, so the enacted text cannot be checked against either index. What follows is the bill as filed, not the law.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 282, copy as filed

readings.whatItDoes:
This creates and establishes an infirmary hospital in Tipo-Tipo, Basilan.

The municipality has 25,531 people across 4,195 households at the 2020 census. The nearest hospital is the Lamitan District Hospital, 22.2 kilometers away by the Basilan Circumferential Road, and patients travel long hours to reach it.
readings.whyProposed:
The note's case is distance and the inadequacy of what lies at the end of it. Tipo-Tipo's patients travel 22.2 kilometers to Lamitan, to a district hospital that another bill in this registry documents as a 25-bed Level I facility with 4 permanent physicians serving a catchment of 100,150 people across 8 municipalities.

So the journey ends at a hospital that is itself over capacity, which is the argument for a facility in the municipality rather than a better road to the existing one.
whoIsAffected: The 25,531 residents of Tipo-Tipo across 4,195 households.
Patients travelling 22.2 kilometers to Lamitan District Hospital.
Lamitan District Hospital, whose catchment already covers 8 municipalities on 25 beds.
The Ministry of Health, which would supervise the infirmary.
implementedBy: Ministry of Health, which would supervise the facility and approve its structure and staffing

funding.detail: No amount is named; the title carries "appropriating funds therefor" and the sum is left to the Bangsamoro appropriations act.

whatChanges: Tipo-Tipo gains an infirmary hospital.
A 22.2-kilometer journey stops being the route to the nearest facility.
Pressure eases on an over-subscribed district hospital in Lamitan.
readings.insight:
This bill needs reading against an act that already exists, and the registry does not connect them. In August 2025 BAA 78 established a 25-bed Level I general hospital in Tipo-Tipo, with ₱50 million from the 2025 budget and a scheme for transferring management to Basilan province once the province can show the capacity to run it. That act began as Bill No. 104, filed by MP Mawallil in October 2022.

This bill was filed in February 2024 — after Bill 104 had been filed and before it was enacted — and proposes an infirmary in the same municipality. It is still listed at Second Reading, Committee Stage, while the measure it overlaps became law. So Tipo-Tipo is the subject of 2 hospital measures from 2 different members, 1 of which is now an act, and neither document refers to the other.

Whether that is duplication or complement depends on a distinction the bills do not draw. An infirmary and a 25-bed Level I general hospital are different facilities — an infirmary is smaller, cheaper and aimed at stabilisation and short stays — and a municipality could sensibly have both, or could have wanted the infirmary as an interim step while the hospital was built. But nothing in this bill positions it that way, and with BAA 78 enacted the practical question is whether this measure now has any work left to do.

That is the recurring cost of the pattern this registry documents: 23 hospital bills from 10 members, converging on the same municipalities without visible coordination, with no mechanism inside Parliament for noticing that a subject is already taken. The Tipo-Tipo pair and the 2 identical orphanage bills are the clearest instances.

readFrom.label: Parliament Bill No. 283, copy as filed, with explanatory note

readings.whatItDoes:
Three sections and one page. This renames the Municipality of Sultan Mastura in Maguindanao del Norte to the Municipality of Subpangen.

Section 2 makes the change conditional: the renaming takes effect only on ratification by a majority of the votes cast by qualified voters in a plebiscite conducted and supervised by COMELEC in the present Municipality of Sultan Mastura. The expenses of that plebiscite are to be borne by the Bangsamoro Government.

The Act takes effect 15 days after publication. There is nothing else in it — no transitional provision for records, seals, signage or contracts held in the old name.
readings.whyProposed:
No explanatory note is attached and the bill offers no reason. Sultan Mastura is named for a historical figure; Subpangen is a place name.

What the bill does say, by requiring a plebiscite, is that the author treated the name of a municipality as belonging to the people who live in it rather than to Parliament. Renaming is within the region's power to legislate over its own political subdivisions, and the choice to put it to a vote anyway is the substantive decision in the document.
whoIsAffected: Residents of Sultan Mastura, who would vote on their municipality's name.
The municipal government, whose records, seal, signage and contracts all carry the existing name.
The Bangsamoro Government, which pays for the plebiscite.
COMELEC, which conducts and supervises it.
implementedBy: Commission on Elections — conduct and supervision of the plebiscite in the present Municipality of Sultan Mastura
The Bangsamoro Government, which bears the plebiscite expenses

funding.detail: No amount is named. The expenses of the plebiscite are borne by the Bangsamoro Government — a departure from the municipality creation bills in this registry, which charge the plebiscite to COMELEC's own appropriations.

whatChanges: Sultan Mastura would become Subpangen, if its voters approve.
The region pays for the plebiscite rather than passing the cost to COMELEC.
readings.insight:
Requiring a plebiscite to change a name is the choice worth noting, and it turns out to be the region's settled practice rather than this bill's innovation. BAA 90, which renamed Datu Blah T. Sinsuat to West Upi in May 2026, does the same thing: it conditions the change on ratification by a majority of the municipality's own voters, in a plebiscite run by COMELEC under the Local Government Code's procedure for changes of name. So on the central question this bill is in line with what Parliament went on to enact.

Who pays is also consistent, and it runs the more principled way. Every municipality *creation* bill in this registry charges the plebiscite to COMELEC's own appropriations — the region spending a national agency's money on a regional decision. This bill has the Bangsamoro Government bear the cost, and BAA 90 charges it to the Contingent Fund of the Office of the Chief Minister. Both put the cost of a regional referendum on the region.

Where this bill falls short of the enacted model is in what it leaves untouched. BAA 90 amends Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 198 — the ARMM-era statute that created the municipality under its original name — so that the renaming reaches the law the name comes from. This bill amends nothing. Sultan Mastura was itself created by an earlier statute, and renaming a municipality without touching the act that named it leaves 2 instruments disagreeing.

What the bill also omits is everything that follows a renaming. A municipality's name appears on its seal, its records, its land titles, its business permits, its road signs and every contract it is party to, and statutes that rename places normally carry a provision saying that references to the old name are read as references to the new one. This one does not, which would leave a genuine question about the continuity of instruments executed as Sultan Mastura.

readings.whatItDoes:
This takes the eight municipalities of the Special Geographic Area — Kadayangan, Kapalawan, Ligawasan, Malidegao, Nabalawag, Old Kaabakan, Pahamuddin and Tugunan — and treats them as one development and administrative area rather than eight separate towns, under the direct supervision of the Chief Minister. The body that runs it, the Special Geographic Area Development Authority, already existed in interim form under the Bangsamoro Administrative Code; this gives it a governing board, a staff structure, defined powers, and money of its own.

The logic of the thing is in its definition of "SGA-wide services": services whose impact crosses town boundaries, or that cost so much no single municipality could provide them. Five are named — development planning; flood control and sewerage; rural, zoning and land use planning and shelter; health and sanitation, environmental protection and pollution control; and public safety, including disaster preparedness and relief for floods, fires and earthquakes. A sixth is open-ended: anything else the Chief Minister may delegate pursuant to a law.

The money is the part that carries furthest. Section 10 authorises ₱500 million for initial operation, then hands the Authority a fixed 5 percent of all revenue the Bangsamoro Government collects, every year, on top of whatever the annual appropriations act gives it. It may also levy fines and charge fees for services it renders.
readings.whyProposed: The bill's own policy section makes the argument: the Special Geographic Area needs to be treated as a special development and administrative area, and certain basic services affecting it are more efficiently planned, supervised and coordinated area-wide than town by town. These are the eight municipalities constituted after the 2019 plebiscite in which 63 barangays of North Cotabato voted to join the Bangsamoro — new units, sharing a marshland basin, with problems that stop at no boundary. An interim Authority was already operating; this puts it on a permanent footing and funds it.
whoIsAffected: Residents of the eight SGA municipalities, for whom flood control, drainage, land use, shelter, health and sanitation, and disaster response become one authority's responsibility rather than eight.

The mayors and councils of those municipalities, whose autonomy over purely local matters is expressly preserved twice in the text, and whose consent SGADA needs before it delivers basic services in their town — but whose development plans must now fit SGADA's master plan.
Employees of the interim SGADA, who keep their duties, salaries and allowances until formally notified of a change, and who are owed 1¼ month's salary for every year of service if displaced.
Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies, whose strategic plans for the area are framed by SGADA's master plan and whose plans route through the planning authority for integration.
Every Bangsamoro taxpayer, because the 5 percent annual share is drawn from region-wide revenue while the services are delivered in eight municipalities.
implementedBy: Special Geographic Area Development Authority (SGADA), under the direct supervision of the Chief Minister

The Special Geographic Area Board — the SGADA Chairperson, the Minister of the Interior and Local Government, the Minister of Finance and Budget and Management, the Bangsamoro Director General of BPDA, and the President of the SGA League of Mayors
An Executive Director and three Deputy Executive Directors for finance and administration, planning, and operations, all appointed by the Chief Minister
The eight component local government units, which carry out much of the implementation
Bangsamoro Planning and Development Authority, which integrates SGADA's plans into the Bangsamoro Development Plan
Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management, and the Commission on Audit, over the transfer of the interim body's assets and liabilities

funding.detail: ₱500,000,000 authorised for initial operation, with annual expenditures and capital outlays thereafter provided in the General Appropriations Act. On top of that the Authority takes a fixed 5 percent annually of all revenue collection of the Bangsamoro Government, and is empowered to levy fines and impose fees and charges for services rendered. The 5 percent share is the unusual term: it is a standing claim on regional revenue rather than a sum voted each year, and the text sets no ceiling and no expiry on it.

whatChanges: The eight SGA municipalities become a single special development and administrative area under the Chief Minister's direct supervision.
The interim Authority becomes a permanent one with a governing board, an Executive Director, three deputies and a staffing pattern.
Area-wide flood control, land use, shelter, health and sanitation, pollution control and disaster response acquire one accountable office.
SGADA's master plan becomes the framework that both Bangsamoro ministry plans and the eight LGU development plans must fit.
The Authority gains ₱500 million to start and a standing 5 percent of annual Bangsamoro revenue thereafter.
The Authority may contract, enter memoranda of agreement, and deal directly with foreign assistance agencies for grants and financing.
Local autonomy over purely local matters is preserved in terms, and SGADA needs an LGU's consent before delivering basic services there.
readings.insight:
Three things are worth watching, and none of them is the stated purpose.

The first is the 5 percent. Almost every other appropriation in the registry is a sum voted for a purpose; this is a permanent slice of regional revenue assigned to one authority serving eight of the region's municipalities, with no ceiling and no sunset in the filed text. Whether that is proportionate is a political question, but it is the provision that will still be doing work in 10 years.

The second is who wrote it. Parliament's own member profile records the principal author, MP Butch P. Malang, as Administrator of the Special Geographic Area and Development Authority since 2022 — the body this bill expands, staffs and funds. The rulebook requires a member to take no part in proceedings on a measure where they hold a conflict of interest or stand to gain or lose financially. Whether that rule was engaged here is not something this registry can determine, and nothing in the published record suggests it was raised; the fact is stated because a reader weighing the bill deserves to know it.

The third is the paperwork. Parliament's index carries this enactment twice — as Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 93 and again as No. 94, same title, same ratification date of 16 July 2026, both tracing back to Bill 431. The bill's own history line on the index closes with 'BAA No. 93', which points to 93 as the operative number and 94 as an indexing artefact. Anyone citing it should quote the date and the title as well as a number.

There is a fourth thing, and it is the reason this reading is of the bill rather than the law. Parliament has not published the signed text of this enactment. Its act pages carry no attachment, and the same is true of the two other acts ratified alongside it (BAA 92 and 94) — the three most recent acts on the index are all text-less as of this capture. So the filed bill is currently the only readable version of this law.

One drafting note on top of that: the filed copy runs Section 8 straight into Section 10. There is no Section 9.
